title: al-Maqṣūd
author: Abū Ḥanīfa (attributed)
subject: sarf
summary: The Maqṣūd (Turkish Maksûd), a short Arabic book of ṣarf traditionally attributed to Abū Ḥanīfa, an attribution many scholars doubt; in the Ottoman madrasa it is read after the Amthila and the Binā and before al-ʿIzzī. Where the Binā lists the patterns, the Maqṣūd teaches how to make the forms: the six forms derived from the maṣdar and their rules, the full conjugation of the sound verb in every pattern with the vowels spelled out, a chapter of useful points on transitivity, the meanings of the added letters and the changes of iftaʿala, and a long last chapter on the weak, doubled and hamzated verbs, with each change (iʿlāl) explained step by step from its base form. The lessons follow its order, show the regular forms with The Nahwi's conjugation tool, and give the weak forms only as the print gives them.

lessons.title: Why taṣrīf; the bare three-letter verb
body: The Maqṣūd opens with praise of God and blessings on the Prophet in rhymed prose (al-ṣawāb, al-adhnāb, al-thawāb, al-aṣḥāb), and then states its purpose in one sentence: “Arabic is a means to the sciences of the sharīʿa, and one of its pillars is taṣrīf, because by it the few verbs become many.” From one root ṣarf makes dozens of forms; the student who knows the rules can read and make them all.

The verbs are of two kinds: original (aṣlī), with root letters only, and with addition (dhū ziyāda). The original verb is three-letter or four-letter. The three-letter verb, “whose past has three letters”, has six bābs, and the book gives each by the vowel of its ʿayn: faʿala yafʿulu, with a fatḥa in the past and a ḍamma in the present (al-ghābir); faʿala yafʿilu, fatḥa and kasra; faʿala yafʿalu, fatḥa in both.

The Maqṣūd's way is short and rule-based: it names the pattern and the vowels, not a model verb for each. The student who has read the Binā already knows the models (naṣara, ḍaraba, fataḥa); the Maqṣūd expects him to supply them. Its title, “the aim”, is that of a book meant to reach what is needed quickly.

The attribution to Abū Ḥanīfa, the founder of the Ḥanafī school, is the madrasa's tradition; many scholars doubt it, and the book itself does not name its author in our print. What is certain is its place: in the Ottoman madrasa it is the third ṣarf book, after the Amthila and the Binā.

tasks.prompt: Give the reason the Maqṣūd gives for studying taṣrīf, and explain it with naṣara.
tasks.answer: Taṣrīf is a pillar of Arabic, the means to the sciences of the sharīʿa, because by it the few verbs become many. From naṣara come yanṣuru, naṣr, nāṣir, manṣūr, unṣur, lam yanṣur and the rest: one root, many forms.

text.original: بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ. الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الْوَهَّابِ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ سَبِيلَ الصَّوَابِ، وَالصَّلَاةُ وَالسَّلَامُ عَلَى نَبِيِّهِ مُحَمَّدٍ الزَّاجِرِ عَنِ الْأَذْنَابِ، الْحَاثِّ عَلَى طَلَبِ الثَّوَابِ، وَعَلَى آلِهِ وَأَصْحَابِهِ خَيْرِ الْآلِ وَخَيْرِ الْأَصْحَابِ.
text.en: In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. Praise be to God, who grants the believers the path of what is right; and blessing and peace upon His Prophet Muḥammad, who restrains from base things and urges to seek reward, and upon his family and his Companions, the best of families and the best of Companions.

text.original: وَبَعْدُ، فَإِنَّ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ وَسِيلَةٌ إِلَى الْعُلُومِ الشَّرْعِيَّةِ، وَأَحَدُ أَرْكَانِهَا التَّصْرِيفُ؛ لِأَنَّهُ بِهِ يَصِيرُ الْقَلِيلُ مِنَ الْأَفْعَالِ كَثِيرًا، وَاللَّهُ الْمُوَفِّقُ وَالْمُرْشِدُ.
text.en: To proceed: Arabic is a means to the sciences of the Sharīʿa, and one of its pillars is conjugation (taṣrīf), for by it the few verbs become many. God is the one who grants success and guides.

text.original: الْأَفْعَالُ عَلَى ضَرْبَيْنِ: أَصْلِيٌّ وَذُو زِيَادَةٍ. فَالْأَصْلِيُّ ثُلَاثِيٌّ وَرُبَاعِيٌّ؛ فَالثُّلَاثِيُّ مَا كَانَ مَاضِيهِ عَلَى ثَلَاثَةِ أَحْرُفٍ، وَهُوَ سِتَّةُ أَبْوَابٍ: الْأَوَّلُ فَعَلَ يَفْعُلُ بِفَتْحِ الْعَيْنِ فِي الْمَاضِي وَضَمِّهَا فِي الْغَابِرِ، الثَّانِي فَعَلَ يَفْعِلُ بِفَتْحِ الْعَيْنِ فِي الْمَاضِي وَكَسْرِهَا فِي الْغَابِرِ، الثَّالِثُ فَعَلَ يَفْعَلُ بِفَتْحِهَا فِيهِمَا،
text.en: The verbs are of two kinds: original (aṣlī) and with addition. The original are triliteral and quadriliteral. The triliteral is that whose past has three letters, and it is six bābs: the first faʿala yafʿulu, with fatḥa on the ʿayn in the past and ḍamma in the ghābir [the muḍāriʿ]; the second faʿala yafʿilu, with fatḥa on the ʿayn in the past and kasra in the ghābir; the third faʿala yafʿalu, with fatḥa in both;

lessons.title: The other three bābs; the four-letter verb
body: The fourth bāb is faʿila yafʿalu, kasra in the past and fatḥa in the present; the fifth faʿula yafʿulu, ḍamma in both; the sixth faʿila yafʿilu, kasra in both. With the three of the last lesson they make the six bābs of the bare verb.

Then the condition of the third bāb, which the Binā also gave: “what belongs to the third bāb has as its ʿayn or its lām one of the letters of the throat”, ḥāʾ, khāʾ, ʿayn, ghayn, hāʾ and hamza. The Maqṣūd adds the exception the Binā leaves out: abā yaʾbā, “to refuse”, which is of this bāb without a throat letter (its alif and its yāʾ are weak, not throat letters), “and it is irregular” (shādhdh).

The four-letter verb, “whose past has four letters”, has one bāb, faʿlala. “And it may be six bābs, called the attached to the four-letter verb”: fawʿala (ḥawqala), faʿwala (jahwara), fayʿala (bayṭara), faʿyala (ʿathyara), faʿlā (salqā) and faʿlala (jalbaba). These are the six of the Binā, in a different order; the Maqṣūd counts them under the four-letter verb rather than as bābs of their own.

The word shādhdh, “irregular”, is worth learning now. A rule in ṣarf holds for what the Arabs said; when a word goes against it, the books record it as shādhdh, keep it, and do not make other words on its model.

text.original: الرَّابِعُ فَعِلَ يَفْعَلُ بِكَسْرِهَا فِي الْمَاضِي وَفَتْحِهَا فِي الْغَابِرِ، الْخَامِسُ فَعُلَ يَفْعُلُ بِضَمِّهَا فِيهِمَا، السَّادِسُ فَعِلَ يَفْعِلُ بِكَسْرِهَا فِي الْمَاضِي وَالْغَابِرِ. وَمَا كَانَ مُخْتَصًّا بِالْبَابِ الثَّالِثِ لَا يَكُونُ إِلَّا عَيْنُهُ أَوْ لَامُهُ حَرْفًا مِنْ حُرُوفِ الْحَلْقِ، إِلَّا أَبَى يَأْبَى، وَهُوَ شَاذٌّ. وَحُرُوفُ الْحَلْقِ سِتَّةٌ: الْحَاءُ وَالْخَاءُ وَالْعَيْنُ وَالْغَيْنُ وَالْهَاءُ وَالْهَمْزَةُ.
text.en: the fourth faʿila yafʿalu, with kasra in the past and fatḥa in the ghābir; the fifth faʿula yafʿulu, with ḍamma in both; the sixth faʿila yafʿilu, with kasra in the past and the ghābir. What belongs to the third bāb has as its ʿayn or its lām only one of the letters of the throat, except abā yaʾbā “to refuse”, which is irregular (shādhdh). The letters of the throat are six: ḥāʾ, khāʾ, ʿayn, ghayn, hāʾ and hamza.

text.original: وَالرُّبَاعِيُّ مَا كَانَ مَاضِيهِ عَلَى أَرْبَعَةِ أَحْرُفٍ، وَهُوَ بَابُ فَعْلَلَ، وَهُوَ بَابٌ وَاحِدٌ، وَقَدْ يَكُونُ سِتَّةَ أَبْوَابٍ يُقَالُ لَهَا: الْمُلْحَقُ بِالرُّبَاعِيِّ، وَهُوَ فَوْعَلَ نَحْوُ حَوْقَلَ، وَفَعْوَلَ نَحْوُ جَهْوَرَ، وَفَيْعَلَ نَحْوُ بَيْطَرَ، وَفَعْيَلَ نَحْوُ عَثْيَرَ، وَفَعْلَى نَحْوُ سَلْقَى، وَفَعْلَلَ نَحْوُ جَلْبَبَ.
text.en: The quadriliteral is that whose past has four letters; it is the bāb of faʿlala, which is a single bāb. There may be six [more] bābs, which are called the forms attached to the quadriliteral: fawʿala, as ḥawqala; faʿwala, as jahwara; fayʿala, as bayṭara; faʿyala, as ʿathyara; faʿlā, as salqā; and faʿlala, as jalbaba.

lessons.title: The augmented verbs counted by their letters
body: The augmented verb is of two kinds: added to the three-letter verb, and added to the four-letter. The Maqṣūd counts fourteen bābs for the first and three for the second, and it sorts them by the number of letters in the past: four-letter (rubāʿī), five-letter (khumāsī) and six-letter (sudāsī).

Four letters, three bābs: afʿala, faʿʿala “with the ʿayn doubled”, and fāʿala. Five letters, five bābs: infaʿala, iftaʿala, ifʿalla “with the lām doubled”, tafaʿʿala and tafāʿala. Six letters, six bābs: istafʿala, ifʿawʿala, ifʿawwala, ifʿanlala, ifʿanlā and ifʿālla. And the augmented four-letter verb has three: ifʿanlala, ifʿalalla and tafaʿlala.

Compare the Binā, which counted twelve augmented three-letter bābs by the number of added letters. The Maqṣūd counts fourteen because it puts ifʿanlala and ifʿanlā (iqʿansasa and islanqā), which the Binā called attached to iḥranjama, among the six-letter forms of the three-letter verb. So ifʿanlala appears twice in its list: once for the three-letter root (iqʿansasa) and once for the four-letter (iḥranjama). Both books describe the same verbs; they file them differently.

Note too the words rubāʿī, khumāsī, sudāsī here: they count the letters of the past, not the root. Akrama is “four-letter” by this count though its root has three letters. Read the word in its context: in one place rubāʿī means a four-letter root, in another a four-letter past.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْمَزِيدُ فِيهِ فَنَوْعَانِ: مَزِيدٌ عَلَى الثُّلَاثِيِّ، وَمَزِيدٌ عَلَى الرُّبَاعِيِّ. فَمَزِيدُ الثُّلَاثِيِّ أَرْبَعَةَ عَشَرَ بَابًا، وَهِيَ ثَلَاثَةُ أَنْوَاعٍ: رُبَاعِيٌّ وَخُمَاسِيٌّ وَسُدَاسِيٌّ. فَالرُّبَاعِيُّ عَلَى ثَلَاثَةِ أَبْوَابٍ: أَفْعَلَ، وَفَعَّلَ بِتَشْدِيدِ الْعَيْنِ، وَفَاعَلَ.
text.en: As for the augmented, it is of two sorts: augmented on the triliteral and augmented on the quadriliteral. The augmented triliteral is fourteen bābs, of three kinds: of four letters, of five and of six. The four-letter are three bābs: afʿala; faʿʿala, with doubling of the ʿayn; and fāʿala.

text.original: وَالْخُمَاسِيُّ خَمْسَةُ أَبْوَابٍ: انْفَعَلَ، وَافْتَعَلَ، وَافْعَلَّ بِتَشْدِيدِ اللَّامِ، وَتَفَعَّلَ بِتَشْدِيدِ الْعَيْنِ، وَتَفَاعَلَ. وَالسُّدَاسِيُّ سِتَّةُ أَبْوَابٍ: اسْتَفْعَلَ، وَافْعَوْعَلَ، وَافْعَوَّلَ بِتَشْدِيدِ الْوَاوِ، وَافْعَنْلَلَ، وَافْعَنْلَى، وَافْعَالَّ بِتَشْدِيدِ اللَّامِ. وَمَزِيدُ الرُّبَاعِيِّ ثَلَاثَةُ أَبْوَابٍ: افْعَنْلَلَ، وَافْعَلَلَّ بِتَشْدِيدِ اللَّامِ الْأَخِيرَةِ، وَتَفَعْلَلَ.
text.en: The five-letter are five bābs: infaʿala, iftaʿala, ifʿalla with doubling of the lām, tafaʿʿala with doubling of the ʿayn, and tafāʿala. The six-letter are six bābs: istafʿala, ifʿawʿala, ifʿawwala with doubling of the wāw, ifʿanlala, ifʿanlā, and ifʿālla with doubling of the lām. The augmented quadriliteral is three bābs: ifʿanlala, ifʿalalla with doubling of the last lām, and tafaʿlala.

parts.title: The forms derived from the maṣdar

lessons.title: The six forms; the maṣdar mīmī and the noun of place
body: The second section names “the forms that most need to be derived from the maṣdar”: six, the past, the present, the imperative, the prohibition, the active participle and the passive participle. The Maqṣūd takes the maṣdar as the source of the verb, the Baṣran view, and builds everything from it.

The maṣdar itself is mīmī or not. If not mīmī, “it is heard (samāʿī)”: every maṣdar is kept as the Arabs said it, “for there is no rule for the maṣdar of the three-letter verb”; the maṣdar of verbs above three letters follows rules (qiyāsī). This is the reason the conjugation tool leaves the bare verb's maṣdar empty.

If mīmī, look at the ʿayn of the present. If it has a fatḥa or a ḍamma, the maṣdar mīmī and the noun of time and place are mafʿal, “with fatḥa on the mīm and the ʿayn and sukūn on the fāʾ”: from yanṣuru, manṣar. Then come the famous exceptions, said with a kasra though the rule wants a fatḥa: al-maṭliʿ (place of rising), al-mankhir (nostril), al-masjid (mosque), al-mansik (place of rites), al-mashriq (east), al-majzir (slaughter place), al-maskin (dwelling), al-manbit (place of growth), al-mafriq (parting of the hair), al-masqiṭ (place of falling), al-majmiʿ (place of gathering).

The list is learnt by heart in the madrasa, and it explains words the student already knows: masjid, “the place of prostration”, from sajada yasjudu, should by rule be masjad, but the Arabs said masjid, and so the books record it among the exceptions.

text.original: وَهِيَ سِتَّةٌ: الْمَاضِي، وَالْمُضَارِعُ، وَالْأَمْرُ، وَالنَّهْيُ، وَاسْمُ الْفَاعِلِ، وَالْمَفْعُولُ. فَأَمَّا الْمَصْدَرُ فَلَا يَخْلُو مِنْ أَنْ يَكُونَ مِيمِيًّا أَوْ غَيْرَ مِيمِيٍّ، فَإِنْ كَانَ غَيْرَ مِيمِيٍّ فَهُوَ سَمَاعِيٌّ، وَنَعْنِي بِالسَّمَاعِيِّ: مَا يُحْفَظُ كُلُّ مَصْدَرٍ عَلَى مَا جَاءَ مِنَ الْعَرَبِ وَلَا يُقَاسُ عَلَيْهِ؛ لِأَنَّهُ لَا قِيَاسَ لِمَصْدَرِ الثُّلَاثِيِّ، وَمَصْدَرُ غَيْرِ الثُّلَاثِيِّ قِيَاسِيٌّ.
text.en: They are six: the past, the muḍāriʿ, the imperative, the prohibition, the active participle and the passive participle. As for the maṣdar, it is either mīmī or not mīmī. If it is not mīmī, it is heard (samāʿī); by heard we mean that each maṣdar is learnt by heart as it has come from the Arabs, and no analogy is drawn from it, for there is no rule for the maṣdar of the triliteral; the maṣdar of what is not triliteral goes by rule (qiyāsī).

text.original: فَإِنْ كَانَ مِيمِيًّا فَيُنْظَرُ فِي عَيْنِ الْفِعْلِ الْمُضَارِعِ، فَإِنْ كَانَ مَفْتُوحًا أَوْ مَضْمُومًا فَالْمَصْدَرُ الْمِيمِيُّ وَالزَّمَانُ وَالْمَكَانُ مِنْهُ مَفْعَلٌ بِفَتْحِ الْمِيمِ وَالْعَيْنِ وَسُكُونِ الْفَاءِ، إِلَّا مَا شَذَّ، نَحْوُ: الْمَطْلِعِ، وَالْمَنْخِرِ، وَالْمَسْجِدِ، وَالْمَنْسِكِ، وَالْمَشْرِقِ، وَالْمَجْزِرِ، وَالْمَسْكِنِ، وَالْمَنْبِتِ، وَالْمَفْرِقِ، وَالْمَسْقِطِ، وَالْمَجْمِعِ، بِكَسْرِ الْعَيْنِ، وَإِنْ كَانَ الْقِيَاسُ الْفَتْحَ.
text.en: If it is mīmī, one looks at the ʿayn of the muḍāriʿ verb: if it has a fatḥa or a ḍamma, the maṣdar mīmī and the [nouns of] time and place from it are mafʿalun, with fatḥa on the mīm and the ʿayn and sukūn on the fāʾ, except what is irregular, as al-maṭliʿi “the place of rising”, al-mankhiri “the nostril”, al-masjidi “the mosque”, al-mansiki “the place of rites”, al-mashriqi “the east”, al-majziri “the place of slaughter”, al-maskini “the dwelling”, al-manbiti “the place of growth”, al-mafriqi “the parting of the hair”, al-masqiṭi “the place of falling” and al-majmiʿi “the place of gathering”, with kasra on the ʿayn, although the rule is the fatḥa.

lessons.title: The mīmī forms in the other cases
body: If the ʿayn of the present has a kasra, the maṣdar mīmī is still mafʿal, “except al-marjiʿ and al-maṣīr, which are maṣdars and came with a kasra”, but the noun of time and place takes a kasra: mafʿil, as in majlis, “a place of sitting”, from yajlisu. “This is in the sound, the hollow, the doubled and the hamzated verb.”

The weak verbs have rules of their own. In the defective verb (nāqiṣ), the maṣdar and the noun of time and place are mafʿal “in all the bābs”, whatever the vowel of the present. In the verb weak in its fāʾ (the mithāl), they are mafʿil in all the bābs. The joined lafīf follows the defective, the separated lafīf follows the mithāl, because each follows the weak letter that matters most at its end or its start.

For the verbs above three letters the rule is short and complete: the maṣdar mīmī, the noun of time and place and the passive participle are all on the pattern of the passive present of that bāb, with the prefix replaced by a mīm with ḍamma; the active participle is the same with a kasra on the ʿayn. From yukramu comes mukram, “honoured” and also “a place or time of honouring”; from yukrimu, mukrim, “one who honours”.

So one form in the augmented verbs can mean four things: mustakhraj is “extracted”, “a place of extracting”, “a time of extracting” and “extracting”. The sentence decides. The conjugation tool gives the passive participle (ismMaful) of each augmented pattern, and by this rule it is the other three as well.

text.original: وَإِنْ كَانَ مَكْسُورًا فَالْمَصْدَرُ الْمِيمِيُّ مِنْهُ مَفْعَلٌ بِفَتْحِ الْمِيمِ وَالْعَيْنِ وَسُكُونِ الْفَاءِ، إِلَّا الْمَرْجِعَ وَالْمَصِيرَ فَإِنَّهُمَا مَصْدَرَانِ وَقَدْ جَاءَا بِكَسْرِ الْعَيْنِ، وَالزَّمَانُ وَالْمَكَانُ مِنْهُ بِكَسْرِ الْعَيْنِ. هَذَا فِي الصَّحِيحِ وَالْأَجْوَفِ وَالْمُضَاعَفِ وَالْمَهْمُوزِ.
text.en: If it has a kasra, the maṣdar mīmī from it is mafʿalun, with fatḥa on the mīm and the ʿayn and sukūn on the fāʾ, except al-marjiʿa “the return” and al-maṣīra “the becoming”, which are two maṣdars that have come with kasra on the ʿayn; and the [nouns of] time and place from it have kasra on the ʿayn. This is in the sound, the hollow, the doubled and the hamzated verb.

text.original: وَأَمَّا فِي النَّاقِصِ فَالْمَصْدَرُ وَالزَّمَانُ وَالْمَكَانُ مِنْهُ مَفْعَلٌ بِفَتْحِ الْمِيمِ وَالْعَيْنِ مِنْ جَمِيعِ الْأَبْوَابِ، وَفِي الْمُعْتَلِّ الْفَاءِ مَفْعِلٌ بِكَسْرِ الْعَيْنِ مِنْ جَمِيعِ الْأَبْوَابِ، وَاللَّفِيفُ الْمَقْرُونُ كَالنَّاقِصِ، وَاللَّفِيفُ الْمَفْرُوقُ كَالْمُعْتَلِّ الْفَاءِ.
text.en: As for the defective (nāqiṣ), the maṣdar and the [nouns of] time and place from it are mafʿalun, with fatḥa on the mīm and the ʿayn, from all the bābs; and in the verb with a weak first letter it is mafʿilun, with kasra on the ʿayn, from all the bābs. The joined lafīf is like the defective, and the separated lafīf like the verb with a weak first letter.

text.original: وَإِنْ كَانَ الْفِعْلُ زَائِدًا عَلَى الثُّلَاثِيِّ فَالْمَصْدَرُ الْمِيمِيُّ وَالزَّمَانُ وَالْمَكَانُ وَالْمَفْعُولُ مِنْ كُلِّ بَابٍ يَكُونُ عَلَى وَزْنِ مُضَارِعِ الْمَجْهُولِ مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْبَابِ، إِلَّا أَنَّكَ تُبْدِلُ حَرْفَ الْمُضَارَعَةِ بِالْمِيمِ الْمَضْمُومَةِ، وَالْفَاعِلُ مِنْهُ بِكَسْرِ الْعَيْنِ.
text.en: If the verb is more than triliteral, the maṣdar mīmī, the [nouns of] time and place and the passive participle from each bāb are on the pattern of the passive muḍāriʿ of that bāb, except that you replace the prefix of the muḍāriʿ with a mīm with ḍamma; and the active participle from it has kasra on the ʿayn.

lessons.title: The past; the hamza of joining
body: The past is active (maʿrūf) or passive (majhūl). In the active its last letter is “fixed on the fatḥa in the singular and the dual, masculine or feminine” (naṣara, naṣarā, naṣarat, naṣaratā), “with ḍamma in the plural of the absent men” (naṣarū), “and with sukūn in the rest” (naṣarna, naṣartu …). This is the rule that the Ājurrūmiyya simplified as “always with fatḥa”. And its first letter has a fatḥa in all bābs, except the five- and six-letter ones that begin with a hamza of joining.

The hamza of joining (hamzat al-waṣl) “stands at the start and falls in connected speech”. The book lists it: the hamza of ibn (son), ibnum, ibna (daughter), imruʾ (man), imraʾa (woman), ithnān and ithnatān (two), ism (name), ist (rump), ayman (in the oath ayman allāhi), the hamza of the past, the maṣdar and the imperative of the five- and six-letter verbs, of the imperative of the bare verb, and the hamza joined to the article al-.

Its vowel at the start is a kasra (ibn, inkasara, istakhraja), with three exceptions: the hamza of the article and of ayman have a fatḥa (al-, ayman); the hamza of the imperative of a verb whose present has a ḍamma on the ʿayn takes a ḍamma to follow it (unṣur); and the hamza of the passive past of the five- and six-letter verbs takes a ḍamma.

A beginner reads every alif at the start of a word as a hamza to be said. The madrasa trains the ear: in wa-stakhraja, fa-nkasara, bi-smi llāhi, the hamza is written as an alif and not said, because something stands before it.

tasks.prompt: Give the ending of the last root letter in each, by the Maqṣūd's rule: naṣarat; naṣarū; naṣartum; naṣarā.
tasks.answer: Naṣarat: fatḥa (singular). Naṣarū: ḍamma (plural of the absent men). Naṣartum: sukūn (the rest). Naṣarā: fatḥa (dual).

tasks.prompt: With which vowel does each begin at the start of speech: ism; unṣur; al-kitāb; istaghfara?
tasks.answer: Ism: kasra. Unṣur: ḍamma (the present yanṣuru has a ḍamma on the ʿayn). Al-kitāb: fatḥa (the article). Istaghfara: kasra.

tasks.prompt: In fa-nkasara and bi-smi llāhi, why is no hamza heard?
tasks.answer: The hamza of joining is said only at the start of speech; here fa- and bi- stand before it, so it falls in connected speech, though the alif stays in writing (in bi-smi it is not written either).

quiz.explanation: The last letter has a fatḥa in the singular and dual, a ḍamma in the men's plural, and a sukūn in the rest: naṣartu.

quiz.prompt: What does the hamza of joining do in connected speech?
quiz.explanation: It stands only at the start.

quiz.prompt: Which word begins with a hamza of joining?
quiz.explanation: Ibn begins with a hamza of joining: it is said when the word starts speech and dropped in the middle.

options: the five- and six-letter ones with a hamza of joining
quiz.explanation: Their past begins with that hamza.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْمَاضِي فَلَا يَخْلُو مِنْ أَنْ يَكُونَ الْفِعْلُ مَعْرُوفًا أَوْ مَجْهُولًا، فَإِنْ كَانَ مَعْرُوفًا فَالْحَرْفُ الْأَخِيرُ مِنَ الْمَاضِي مَبْنِيٌّ عَلَى الْفَتْحِ فِي الْوَاحِدِ وَالتَّثْنِيَةِ، سَوَاءٌ كَانَتْ مُذَكَّرًا أَوْ مُؤَنَّثًا، وَمَضْمُومٌ فِي جَمْعِ الْمُذَكَّرِ الْغَائِبِ، وَسَاكِنٌ فِي الْبَوَاقِي مِنْ جَمِيعِ الْأَبْوَابِ، وَالْحَرْفُ الْأَوَّلُ مِنْهُ مَفْتُوحٌ مِنْ جَمِيعِ الْأَبْوَابِ، إِلَّا مِنْ أَبْوَابِ الْخُمَاسِيِّ وَالسُّدَاسِيِّ الَّتِي فِي أَوَّلِهَا هَمْزَةُ الْوَصْلِ.
text.en: As for the past, the verb is either active (maʿrūf) or passive. If it is active, the last letter of the past is fixed on the fatḥa in the singular and the dual, whether masculine or feminine; it has a ḍamma in the plural of the masculine absent, and a sukūn in the rest, in all the bābs. Its first letter has a fatḥa in all the bābs, except in the bābs of five and six letters that begin with the hamza of connection (hamzat al-waṣl).

text.original: وَهَمْزَةُ الْوَصْلِ تَثْبُتُ فِي الِابْتِدَاءِ وَتَسْقُطُ فِي الدَّرْجِ. وَهَمْزَةُ الْوَصْلِ: هَمْزَةُ ابْنٍ، وَابْنُمٍ، وَابْنَةٍ، وَامْرِئٍ، وَامْرَأَةٍ، وَاثْنَيْنِ، وَاثْنَتَيْنِ، وَاسْمٍ، وَاسْتٍ، وَايْمُنٍ، وَهَمْزَةُ الْمَاضِي وَالْمَصْدَرِ وَالْأَمْرِ مِنَ الْخُمَاسِيِّ وَالسُّدَاسِيِّ، وَأَمْرِ الْحَاضِرِ مِنَ الثُّلَاثِيِّ، وَالْهَمْزَةُ الْمُتَّصِلَةُ بِلَامِ التَّعْرِيفِ.
text.en: The hamza of connection stays at the beginning [of speech] and falls away in the course of speech. The hamza of connection is the hamza of ibnin “son”, ibnumin “son”, ibnatin “daughter”, imriʾin “man”, imraʾatin “woman”, ithnayni “two”, ithnatayni “two (f.)”, ismin “name”, istin “buttocks” and aymun “[by] the oath”; and the hamza of the past, the maṣdar and the imperative of the five- and six-letter verbs, of the imperative of the present from the triliteral, and the hamza joined to the lām of the article.

text.original: وَهَمْزَةُ الْوَصْلِ الْمَحْذُوفَةُ فِي الدَّرْجِ مَكْسُورَةٌ فِي الِابْتِدَاءِ، إِلَّا مَا اتَّصَلَتْ بِلَامِ التَّعْرِيفِ وَهَمْزَةَ ايْمُنٍ فَإِنَّهُمَا مَفْتُوحَتَانِ فِي الِابْتِدَاءِ، وَمَا يَكُونُ فِي أَوَّلِ الْأَمْرِ مِنْ يَفْعُلُ بِضَمِّ الْعَيْنِ فَإِنَّهَا مَضْمُومَةٌ فِي الِابْتِدَاءِ تَبَعًا لِلْعَيْنِ، وَكَذَلِكَ مَضْمُومَةٌ فِي الْمَاضِي الْمَجْهُولِ مِنَ الْخُمَاسِيِّ وَالسُّدَاسِيِّ.
text.en: The hamza of connection that is dropped in the course of speech has a kasra at the beginning, except that joined to the lām of the article and the hamza of aymun, for these two have a fatḥa at the beginning; and that at the beginning of the imperative of yafʿulu, with ḍamma on the ʿayn, for it has a ḍamma at the beginning, following the ʿayn; and it likewise has a ḍamma in the passive past of the five- and six-letter verbs.

lessons.title: The passive past; the present
body: The passive past in one sentence: “its last letter is as it was in the active, the letter before the last has a kasra, a letter with sukūn stays as it is, and the rest take a ḍamma.” This general rule covers every bāb at once: nuṣira; ukrima; ustukhrija, “it was extracted”, where every vowelled letter before the last-but-one takes a ḍamma, the hamza of joining included.

The present is the verb that begins with one of the letters of atayna (the same four letters as anaytu, in another order), “on condition that the letter is added to the past”. The prefix has a fatḥa in the active of all bābs, “except in the four-letter verb, whatever four-letter verb it is”: yukrimu, yufarriḥu, yuqātilu, yudaḥriju, all four-letter in the past. The letter before the lām has a kasra in the four-, five- and six-letter verbs (yukrimu, yankasiru, yastakhriju), except in tafaʿʿala, tafāʿala and tafaʿlala, where it has a fatḥa (yatakallamu, yatabāʿadu, yatadaḥraju).

In the passive present the prefix has a ḍamma, a letter with sukūn stays, and “all the rest have a fatḥa” except the lām, which is in rafʿ in active and passive alike until a governor of naṣb or jazm enters: yunṣaru, yukramu, yustakhraju.
The two rules let the student make the passive of any verb from its active, without a table: it is the work the Amthila did for one verb, done once for all.

tasks.answer: Passive past: ustughfira (the last letter as in the active, kasra before it, the sukūn of the sīn kept, ḍamma on the rest). Passive present: yustaghfaru. The tool gives the same.

tasks.prompt: Which vowel does the prefix of the active present take in each: yaktubu, yukrimu, yatadaḥraju (tadaḥraja), yudaḥriju?
tasks.answer: Yaktubu: fatḥa. Yukrimu: ḍamma (four-letter past). Yatadaḥraju: fatḥa (five-letter). Yudaḥriju: ḍamma (four-letter past).

tasks.prompt: Why is the letter before the lām vowelled with fatḥa in yatakallamu but with kasra in yankasiru?
tasks.answer: The Maqṣūd's rule: that letter has a kasra in the four-, five- and six-letter verbs, except in tafaʿʿala, tafāʿala and tafaʿlala, which keep a fatḥa. Takallama is tafaʿʿala; inkasara is infaʿala.

quiz.explanation: In the passive past the letter before the last takes a kasra, a quiescent letter stays, the rest take a ḍamma: nuṣira, ukrima.

quiz.explanation: Ustukhrija: the sīn keeps its sukūn.

quiz.explanation: Yukrimu, yuqātilu, yudaḥriju.

quiz.explanation: Tafaʿʿala, tafāʿala and tafaʿlala.

quiz.explanation: The same four as anaytu.

quiz.explanation: Ḍamma on every vowelled letter before the last-but-one, the hamza included.

text.original: وَإِنْ كَانَ الْفِعْلُ مَجْهُولًا فَالْحَرْفُ الْأَخِيرُ مِنْهُ يَكُونُ مِثْلَ مَا كَانَ فِي الْمَعْرُوفِ، وَالْحَرْفُ الَّذِي قَبْلَ الْأَخِيرِ مَكْسُورَةٌ، وَالسَّاكِنُ سَاكِنٌ عَلَى حَالِهِ، وَمَا بَقِيَ مَضْمُومٌ.
text.en: If the verb is passive, its last letter is as it was in the active; the letter before the last has a kasra; an unvowelled letter stays unvowelled as it was; and the rest have a ḍamma.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْمُضَارِعُ فَهُوَ الَّذِي يَكُونُ فِي أَوَّلِهِ حَرْفٌ مِنْ حُرُوفِ أَتَيْنَ، بِشَرْطِ أَنْ يَكُونَ ذَلِكَ الْحَرْفُ زَائِدًا عَلَى الْمَاضِي. وَحُرُوفُ الْمُضَارَعَةِ مَفْتُوحٌ فِي الْمَعْرُوفِ مِنْ جَمِيعِ الْأَبْوَابِ، إِلَّا مِنَ الرُّبَاعِيِّ أَيَّ رُبَاعِيٍّ كَانَ فَإِنَّهَا مَضْمُومَةٌ فِيهِ، وَمَا قَبْلَ لَامِ فِعْلِ الْمُضَارِعِ مَكْسُورَةٌ فِي الرُّبَاعِيِّ وَالْخُمَاسِيِّ وَالسُّدَاسِيِّ، إِلَّا مِنْ تَفَعَّلَ وَتَفَاعَلَ وَتَفَعْلَلَ فَإِنَّهَا مَفْتُوحَةٌ فِيهِنَّ.
text.en: As for the muḍāriʿ, it is that which has at its beginning one of the letters of atayna, on condition that this letter is added to the past. The prefixes of the muḍāriʿ have a fatḥa in the active of all the bābs, except in the four-letter verb, whatever four-letter verb it is, for in it they have a ḍamma. The letter before the lām of the muḍāriʿ has a kasra in the four-, five- and six-letter verbs, except in tafaʿʿala, tafāʿala and tafaʿlala, for in these it has a fatḥa.

text.original: وَفِي الْمَجْهُولِ حَرْفُ الْمُضَارَعَةِ مَضْمُومٌ، وَالسَّاكِنُ سَاكِنٌ عَلَى حَالِهِ، وَمَا بَقِيَ مَفْتُوحٌ كُلُّهُ غَيْرَ لَامِ الْفِعْلِ، فَإِنَّهَا مَرْفُوعَةٌ فِي الْمَعْرُوفِ وَالْمَجْهُولِ مَا لَمْ يَكُنْ حَرْفٌ نَاصِبٌ يَنْصِبُهَا أَوْ جَازِمٌ يَجْزِمُهَا.
text.en: In the passive, the prefix of the muḍāriʿ has a ḍamma, an unvowelled letter stays unvowelled as it was, and all the rest have a fatḥa except the lām of the verb, which is in rafʿ in the active and the passive as long as there is no particle of naṣb to put it in naṣb or of jazm to put it in jazm.

lessons.title: Command and prohibition
body: “The command and the prohibition are on the form of the present, except that both are in jazm.” The sign of jazm is the dropping of the nūn in the dual, the plural of the men and the woman addressed (li-yanṣurā, lā tanṣurū, unṣurī), the sukūn on a sound lām and the dropping of a weak lām in the rest (li-yanṣur; of the weak verb, the next chapter), except the nūn of the women, which stays “in jazm and elsewhere” (li-yanṣurna, unṣurna).

The command to the one present (amr al-ḥāḍir) in the active is made from the present by dropping the prefix. If the letter after the prefix has a sukūn, a hamza of joining is brought in: taḍribu → iḍrib, tanṣuru → unṣur. If it has a vowel, nothing is needed and only the end is made quiescent: tukrimu → akrim, as the Binā's akrim shows, tudaḥriju → daḥrij, tataʿallamu → taʿallam.

Then a point of doctrine: the imperative “is fixed on the pause (mabnī ʿalā al-waqf), and what is fixed on the pause is like the majzūm in pronunciation”. This is the Baṣran view, which the Ājurrūmiyya does not follow: for the Ājurrūmiyya the imperative is majzūm; for the Maqṣūd it only sounds like it. Both books give the same forms.

The prohibition, and the command to the absent, keep their prefix: lā tanṣur, li-yanṣur. Only the command to the one present in the active loses it; the passive command to the one present keeps it with the lām, li-tunṣar, as the Amthila showed.

tasks.prompt: What is the sign of jazm in each command: li-yanṣurū; li-yanṣur; li-yanṣurna?
tasks.answer: Li-yanṣurū: the dropping of the nūn. Li-yanṣur: the sukūn on the sound lām. Li-yanṣurna: none; the nūn of the women stays.

tasks.prompt: How do the Ājurrūmiyya and the Maqṣūd differ on the imperative?
tasks.answer: The Ājurrūmiyya says the imperative is always majzūm (the Kūfan view). The Maqṣūd says it is fixed on the pause, and only like the majzūm in pronunciation (the Baṣran view). The forms are the same.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْأَمْرُ وَالنَّهْيُ فَإِنَّهُمَا يَكُونَانِ عَلَى لَفْظِ الْمُضَارِعِ إِلَّا أَنَّهُمَا مَجْزُومَانِ، وَعَلَامَةُ الْجَزْمِ فِيهِمَا سُقُوطُ نُونِ التَّثْنِيَةِ وَجَمْعِ الْمُذَكَّرِ وَالْوَاحِدَةِ الْمُخَاطَبَةِ، وَفِي الْبَوَاقِي سُكُونُ لَامِ الْفِعْلِ الصَّحِيحِ وَسُقُوطُ لَامِ الْفِعْلِ الْمُعْتَلِّ، سِوَى نُونِ جَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ فَإِنَّ نُونَهَا ثَابِتَةٌ فِي الْجَزْمِ وَغَيْرِهِ.
text.en: As for the imperative and the prohibition, they are in the wording of the muḍāriʿ, except that they are majzūm. The sign of jazm in them is the falling away of the nūn of the dual, of the masculine plural and of the single feminine addressed; and in the rest, the sukūn of the lām of a sound verb and the falling away of the lām of a weak verb; except the nūn of the feminine plural, for its nūn stays, in jazm and elsewhere.

text.original: وَأَمْرُ الْحَاضِرِ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ تَحْذِفُ مِنْهُ حَرْفَ الْمُضَارَعَةِ وَتُدْخِلُ هَمْزَةَ الْوَصْلِ إِنْ كَانَ مَا بَعْدَ حَرْفِ الْمُضَارَعَةِ سَاكِنًا، وَإِنْ كَانَ مُتَحَرِّكًا فَتُسَكِّنُ آخِرَهُ، وَهُوَ مَبْنِيٌّ عَلَى الْوَقْفِ، وَالْمَبْنِيُّ عَلَى الْوَقْفِ كَالْمَجْزُومِ فِي اللَّفْظِ.
text.en: The active imperative of the present: you drop from it the prefix of the muḍāriʿ, and bring in the hamza of connection if what follows the prefix is unvowelled; if it is vowelled, you [only] put a sukūn on its end. It is fixed on the pause (mabnī ʿalā al-waqf), and what is fixed on the pause is like the majzūm in pronunciation.

lessons.title: The participles and the intensive patterns
body: For the active participle of the bare verb “look at the ʿayn of the past”. If it has a fatḥa, the pattern is nāṣir (fāʿil). If it has a ḍamma, the adjective is on ʿaẓīm or ḍakhm (faʿīl, faʿl): a verb like karuma names a lasting quality, and its describing word is not a participle on fāʿil. If it has a kasra: from the transitive, ʿālim (fāʿil); from the intransitive, four patterns: marīḍ (ill), zamin (chronically ill), aḥmar (red) and ʿaṭshān (thirsty).

The book gives their feminines, duals and plurals in full, for they are irregular in ways a beginner cannot guess: aḥmar, feminine ḥamrāʾ, plural of both ḥumr; duals aḥmarāni and ḥamrāwāni. ʿAṭshān, feminine ʿaṭshā, plural of both ʿiṭāsh; duals ʿaṭshānāni and ʿaṭshayāni. “I have kept to what can be fixed by rule of the active participle and left the rest.”

The passive participle of every bare verb is majbūr (mafʿūl), and also kasīr (faʿīl, with the sense of mafʿūl, “broken”). For the augmented verbs both participles were given with the maṣdar mīmī (lesson 5). Then the patterns of intensity (mubālagha): jahūl (very ignorant), ṣiddīq (very truthful), kadhdhāb (great liar), ghufl, yaquẓ (very alert), midrār (pouring much), mikthīr, and luʿana (one who curses much); “if you put a sukūn on the ʿayn of the last pattern, it takes the sense of the passive”: luʿna, one much cursed.

The lesson connects with what the student knows: the Amthila had one intensive, naṣṣār; here are eight patterns; and the ʿAwāmil showed the ṣifa mushabbaha (ḥasan) at work. The bare verb's adjectives are many-shaped, and the Maqṣūd teaches only what a rule can hold.

tasks.answer: Aḥmar: feminine ḥamrāʾ; duals aḥmarāni, ḥamrāwāni; plural of both ḥumr. ʿAṭshān: feminine ʿaṭshā; duals ʿaṭshānāni, ʿaṭshayāni; plural of both ʿiṭāsh.

tasks.prompt: Why is the adjective of a verb on faʿula (karuma, ʿaẓuma) not on fāʿil?
tasks.answer: Verbs of that bāb name lasting qualities and are intransitive; their adjectives are of the kind the ʿAwāmil called the ṣifa mushabbaha, on patterns such as faʿīl (ʿaẓīm, karīm) and faʿl (ḍakhm).

tasks.prompt: What is the difference between luʿana and luʿna?
tasks.answer: Luʿana, with a fatḥa on the ʿayn, is one who curses much (intensive, active sense). With a sukūn, luʿna, it takes the passive sense: one who is much cursed.

quiz.prompt: For the active participle of the bare verb, the Maqṣūd looks at…
quiz.explanation: Fatḥa, ḍamma or kasra.

quiz.prompt: The adjective of a verb with ḍamma in the past is on…
quiz.explanation: A verb with ḍamma in its past, such as ʿaẓuma, gives an adjective on faʿīl or faʿl: ʿaẓīm, ḍakhm.

quiz.prompt: What is the feminine of aḥmar?
quiz.explanation: Aḥmar has the feminine ḥamrāʾ, with madd; the plural of both is ḥumr.

quiz.prompt: What is the plural of ʿaṭshān?
quiz.explanation: Plural of both ʿaṭshān and ʿaṭshā.

quiz.prompt: The passive participle of every bare verb is on…
options: majbūr (mafʿūl), and also faʿīl as kasīr
quiz.explanation: Kasīr: faʿīl with the sense of mafʿūl.

quiz.prompt: Which is a pattern of intensity?
quiz.explanation: Ṣiddīq, very truthful, is one of the book's patterns of intensity, with jahūl and kadhdhāb.

quiz.prompt: What happens to luʿana with a sukūn on the ʿayn?
quiz.explanation: Luʿana means one who curses much; with a quiescent ʿayn, luʿna, it takes the passive sense: much cursed.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْفَاعِلُ فَيُنْظَرُ فِي عَيْنِ الْفِعْلِ الْمَاضِي، فَإِنْ كَانَ مَفْتُوحًا فَوَزْنُهُ نَاصِرٌ، وَإِنْ كَانَ مَضْمُومًا فَوَزْنُهُ عَظِيمٌ وَضَخْمٌ، وَإِنْ كَانَ مَكْسُورًا فَوَزْنُهُ مِنَ الْمُتَعَدِّي عَالِمٌ، وَمِنَ اللَّازِمِ يَأْتِي عَلَى أَرْبَعَةِ أَوْزَانٍ: مَرِيضٌ، وَزَمِنٌ بِفَتْحِ الزَّاءِ وَكَسْرِ الْمِيمِ، وَأَحْمَرُ لِلْمُذَكَّرِ وَحَمْرَاءُ لِلْمُؤَنَّثِ بِالْمَدِّ، وَجَمْعُهُمَا حُمْرٌ بِضَمِّ الْحَاءِ وَسُكُونِ الْمِيمِ،
text.en: As for the active participle, one looks at the ʿayn of the past verb: if it has a fatḥa, its pattern is nāṣirun “helper”; if it has a ḍamma, its pattern is ʿaẓīmun “great” and ḍakhmun “huge”; if it has a kasra, its pattern from the transitive is ʿālimun “knowing”, and from the intransitive it comes on four patterns: marīḍun “sick”; zaminun “chronically ill”, with fatḥa on the zāy and kasra on the mīm; aḥmaru “red” for the masculine and ḥamrāʾu for the feminine, with the long vowel (madd), and their plural is ḥumrun, with ḍamma on the ḥāʾ and sukūn on the mīm;

text.original: وَتَثْنِيَةُ أَحْمَرَ أَحْمَرَانِ، وَتَثْنِيَةُ حَمْرَاءَ حَمْرَاوَانِ، وَعَطْشَانُ لِلْمُذَكَّرِ، وَتَثْنِيَةُ عَطْشَانَ عَطْشَانَانِ، وَعَطْشَى بِفَتْحِ الْعَيْنِ وَسُكُونِ الطَّاءِ وَبِالْقَصْرِ لِلْمُؤَنَّثِ، وَجَمْعُهُمَا عِطَاشٌ بِكَسْرِ الْعَيْنِ، وَتَثْنِيَةُ عَطْشَى عَطْشَيَانِ. وَاخْتَصَرْتُ بِذِكْرِ مَا يُمْكِنُ ضَبْطُهُ مِنَ الْفَاعِلِ وَتَرَكْتُ مَا عَدَاهُ.
text.en: the dual of aḥmara is aḥmarāni, and the dual of ḥamrāʾa is ḥamrāwāni; and ʿaṭshānu “thirsty” for the masculine, whose dual is ʿaṭshānāni, and ʿaṭshā, with fatḥa on the ʿayn, sukūn on the ṭāʾ and the short ending (qaṣr), for the feminine, and their plural is ʿiṭāshun, with kasra on the ʿayn; and the dual of ʿaṭshā is ʿaṭshayāni. I have kept to mentioning what of the active participle can be held by rule, and left aside the rest.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْمَفْعُولُ مِنْ جَمِيعِ الثُّلَاثِيِّ فَوَزْنُهُ مَجْبُورٌ وَكَسِيرٌ، وَقَدْ ذَكَرْنَا الْفَاعِلَ وَالْمَفْعُولَ مِنَ الزَّائِدِ عَلَى الثُّلَاثِيِّ فِي الْمَصْدَرِ الْمِيمِيِّ. وَأَوْزَانُ الْمُبَالَغَةِ: جَهُولٌ، وَصِدِّيقٌ، وَكَذَّابٌ، وَغُفُلٌ بِضَمِّ الْغَيْنِ وَالْفَاءِ، وَيَقُظٌ بِفَتْحِ الْيَاءِ وَضَمِّ الْقَافِ، وَمِدْرَارٌ، وَمِكْثِيرٌ، وَلُعَنَةٌ بِضَمِّ اللَّامِ وَفَتْحِ الْعَيْنِ، فَإِنْ أَسْكَنْتَ الْعَيْنَ مِنَ الْوَزْنِ الْأَخِيرِ يَصِيرُ بِمَعْنَى الْمَفْعُولِ.
text.en: As for the passive participle from all the triliterals, its pattern is majbūrun “set [of a bone]” and kasīrun “broken”. We have mentioned the active and passive participles of what is more than triliteral under the maṣdar mīmī. The intensive patterns are: jahūlun “very ignorant”, ṣiddīqun “very truthful”, kadhdhābun “great liar”, ghufulun “heedless”, with ḍamma on the ghayn and the fāʾ, yaquẓun “wide awake”, with fatḥa on the yāʾ and ḍamma on the qāf, midrārun “pouring abundantly”, mikthīrun “saying much” and luʿanatun “one who curses much”, with ḍamma on the lām and fatḥa on the ʿayn; if you put a sukūn on the ʿayn of the last pattern, it takes the meaning of the passive [one much cursed].

parts.title: The conjugation of the sound verbs

lessons.title: The fourteen forms; the nūn of emphasis
body: The section on the sound verbs begins with the count of forms. The past, the present (here called al-mustaqbal), the command and the prohibition, active and passive, each run through fourteen forms: three of the absent man, three of the absent woman, three of the man addressed, three of the woman addressed, and two of the speaker, “man or woman”. But the active command and prohibition have no forms of the speaker, since one does not order oneself; the Amthila's tables showed the same.

The active participle has ten forms, “of which the plural of the men has four words” (nāṣirūna, nuṣṣār, nuṣṣar, naṣara) “and the plural of the women two” (nāṣirāt, nawāṣir). The passive participle has seven, with two plurals for the men (manṣūrūna, manāṣir) and one for the women (manṣūrāt). The Amthila's tables are thus counted and explained.

Then the nūn of emphasis (nūn al-taʾkīd), which strengthens a command or a prohibition, active or passive. It is heavy, -anna, or light, -an; the light one does not enter the dual and the plural of the women. The light nūn has a sukūn; the heavy one a fatḥa, except in the dual and the women's plural, where it has a kasra (li-yanṣurānni, li-yanṣurnānni). Before it the verb takes a kasra for the woman addressed (unṣurinna), a ḍamma for the men (li-yanṣurunna), and a fatḥa elsewhere (li-yanṣuranna).

The book then gives the examples on naṣara: the past, the present, the commands and prohibitions with “etc.” (ilakh), since the Amthila has given them in full, and the forms with the heavy and the light nūn: li-yanṣuranna, li-yanṣurānni, li-yanṣurunna, li-tanṣuranna, li-tanṣurānni, li-yanṣurnānni, unṣuranna, unṣurānni, unṣurunna, unṣurinna, unṣurānni, unṣurnānni; and li-yanṣuran, li-yanṣurun, li-tanṣuran, unṣuran, unṣurun, unṣurin. These forms are not in the conjugation tool; learn them from the print.

terms.en: here: the present (muḍāriʿ)
the heavy nūn of emphasis: -anna
the light nūn of emphasis: -an
“etc.”: the rest as in the tables

examples.en: li-yanṣuranna, li-yanṣurunna, unṣurinna: fatḥa, ḍamma, kasra before the heavy nūn
the heavy nūn with kasra in the dual and the plural of the women
li-yanṣuran, unṣurun: the light nūn with sukūn

tasks.prompt: Why do the active command and prohibition have no forms of the speaker?
tasks.answer: Because one does not command or forbid oneself in the active; the passive command does have them (li-unṣar, li-nunṣar), as the Amthila showed.

tasks.prompt: Give the vowel of the nūn of emphasis and of the letter before it in: unṣuranna; unṣurinna; unṣurunna; unṣurānni.
tasks.answer: Unṣuranna: nūn with fatḥa, fatḥa before it. Unṣurinna: fatḥa on the nūn, kasra before it (the woman addressed). Unṣurunna: fatḥa on the nūn, ḍamma before it (the men). Unṣurānni: kasra on the nūn (the dual).

tasks.prompt: Count the ten forms of the active participle of naṣara as the book counts them.
tasks.answer: Nāṣir, nāṣirāni, and four plurals for the men (nāṣirūna, nuṣṣār, nuṣṣar, naṣara); nāṣira, nāṣiratāni, and two plurals for the women (nāṣirāt, nawāṣir): ten.

tasks.prompt: Into which forms does the light nūn not enter?
tasks.answer: The dual and the plural of the women.

quiz.prompt: What does the Maqṣūd call the present in this section?
quiz.explanation: It uses several names for the muḍāriʿ.

quiz.prompt: How many forms has the active participle?
quiz.explanation: With four plurals for the men and two for the women.

quiz.prompt: How many forms has the passive participle?
quiz.explanation: Two plurals for the men, one for the women.

quiz.prompt: The heavy nūn has a kasra in…
options: the dual and the plural of the women
quiz.explanation: Li-yanṣurānni, li-yanṣurnānni.

quiz.prompt: Before the nūn of emphasis, the verb takes a ḍamma in…
quiz.explanation: Before the nūn of emphasis comes a kasra for the woman addressed, a ḍamma in the men's plural, a fatḥa elsewhere: li-yanṣurunna.

quiz.prompt: The light nūn of emphasis has…
quiz.explanation: The light nūn is quiescent, li-yanṣuran; the heavy one has a fatḥa, li-yanṣuranna, but a kasra in the dual and women's plural.

quiz.prompt: Which forms have no speaker?
quiz.explanation: One does not order oneself.

text.original: يَتَصَرَّفُ الْمَاضِي وَالْمُسْتَقْبَلُ وَالْأَمْرُ وَالنَّهْيُ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ وَالْمَجْهُولِ عَلَى أَرْبَعَةَ عَشَرَ وَجْهًا: ثَلَاثَةٌ لِلْغَائِبِ، وَثَلَاثَةٌ لِلْغَائِبَةِ، وَثَلَاثَةٌ لِلْمُخَاطَبِ، وَثَلَاثَةٌ لِلْمُخَاطَبَةِ، وَوَجْهَانِ لِلْمُتَكَلِّمِ رَجُلًا كَانَ أَوِ امْرَأَةً، غَيْرَ أَنَّهُ لَا يَأْتِي الْوَجْهَانِ لِلْمُتَكَلِّمِ فِي الْمَعْرُوفِ مِنَ الْأَمْرِ وَالنَّهْيِ.
text.en: The past, the future (mustaqbal), the imperative and the prohibition, active and passive, are conjugated in fourteen forms: three for the absent man, three for the absent woman, three for the man addressed, three for the woman addressed, and two for the speaker, whether man or woman; except that the two forms of the speaker do not come in the active of the imperative and the prohibition.

text.original: وَالْفَاعِلُ يَتَصَرَّفُ عَلَى عَشَرَةِ أَوْجُهٍ، مِنْهَا جَمْعُ الْمُذَكَّرِ أَرْبَعَةُ أَلْفَاظٍ، وَجَمْعُ الْمُؤَنَّثِ لَفْظَانِ. وَالْمَفْعُولُ يَتَصَرَّفُ عَلَى سَبْعَةِ أَوْجُهٍ، مِنْهَا جَمْعُ الْمُذَكَّرِ لَفْظَانِ، وَجَمْعُ الْمُؤَنَّثِ لَفْظٌ وَاحِدٌ.
text.en: The active participle is conjugated in ten forms, of which the masculine plural has four words and the feminine plural two. The passive participle is conjugated in seven forms, of which the masculine plural has two words and the feminine plural one.

text.original: وَنُونُ التَّأْكِيدِ تَدْخُلُ عَلَى جَمِيعِ الْأَمْرِ وَالنَّهْيِ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ وَالْمَجْهُولِ، وَالْمُخَفَّفَةُ كَذَلِكَ غَيْرَ أَنَّهَا لَا تَدْخُلُ فِي التَّثْنِيَةِ وَجَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ. وَالْمُخَفَّفَةُ سَاكِنَةٌ، وَالْمُشَدَّدَةُ مَفْتُوحَةٌ إِلَّا فِي التَّثْنِيَةِ وَجَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ فَإِنَّهَا مَكْسُورَةٌ فِيهِمَا، وَمَا قَبْلَهَا مَكْسُورَةٌ فِي الْوَاحِدَةِ الْحَاضِرَةِ، وَمَضْمُومٌ فِي جَمْعِ الْمُذَكَّرِ، وَمَفْتُوحٌ فِي الْبَوَاقِي.
text.en: The nūn of emphasis comes on the whole of the imperative and the prohibition, active and passive; and the light [nūn] likewise, except that it does not come in the dual and the feminine plural. The light one has a sukūn, and the heavy one a fatḥa, except in the dual and the feminine plural, where it has a kasra. The letter before it has a kasra in the singular feminine present, a ḍamma in the masculine plural, and a fatḥa in the rest.

text.original: مِثَالُ الْمَاضِي: نَصَرَ نَصَرَا نَصَرُوا إِلَخْ، وَمِنَ الْمَجْهُولِ: نُصِرَ نُصِرَا نُصِرُوا إِلَخْ. وَمِثَالُ الْمُسْتَقْبَلِ: يَنْصُرُ يَنْصُرَانِ يَنْصُرُونَ إِلَخْ، وَمِنَ الْمَجْهُولِ: يُنْصَرُ يُنْصَرَانِ يُنْصَرُونَ إِلَخْ. مِثَالُ الْأَمْرِ الْغَائِبِ: لِيَنْصُرْ لِيَنْصُرَا لِيَنْصُرُوا إِلَخْ. مِثَالُ أَمْرِ الْحَاضِرِ: اُنْصُرْ اُنْصُرَا اُنْصُرُوا اُنْصُرِي اُنْصُرَا اُنْصُرْنَ، وَمِنَ الْمَجْهُولِ: لِتُنْصَرْ لِتُنْصَرَا لِتُنْصَرُوا إِلَخْ. وَكَذَلِكَ النَّهْيُ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ وَالْمَجْهُولِ، إِلَّا أَنَّهُ تَزِيدُ فِي أَوَّلِهِ لَا.
text.en: Example of the past: naṣara naṣarā naṣarū “he helped, they two helped, they helped” etc.; and of the passive: nuṣira nuṣirā nuṣirū etc. Example of the future: yanṣuru yanṣurāni yanṣurūna etc.; and of the passive: yunṣaru yunṣarāni yunṣarūna etc. Example of the command to the absent: li-yanṣur li-yanṣurā li-yanṣurū etc. Example of the command to the one present: unṣur unṣurā unṣurū unṣurī unṣurā unṣurna; and of the passive: li-tunṣar li-tunṣarā li-tunṣarū etc. The prohibition, active and passive, is likewise, except that you add lā at its beginning.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي النُّونِ الْمُشَدَّدَةِ: لِيَنْصُرَنَّ لِيَنْصُرَانِّ لِيَنْصُرُنَّ لِتَنْصُرَنَّ لِتَنْصُرَانِّ لِيَنْصُرْنَانِّ، اُنْصُرَنَّ اُنْصُرَانِّ اُنْصُرُنَّ اُنْصُرِنَّ اُنْصُرَانِّ اُنْصُرْنَانِّ. وَفِي الْخَفِيفَةِ: لِيَنْصُرَنْ بِفَتْحِ الرَّاءِ فِي الْوَاحِدِ الْمُذَكَّرِ، لِيَنْصُرُنْ بِضَمِّهَا فِي جَمْعِ الْمُذَكَّرِ، لِتَنْصُرَنْ بِفَتْحِ الرَّاءِ فِي الْوَاحِدَةِ الْغَائِبَةِ، وَفِي الْمُخَاطَبِ: اُنْصُرَنْ اُنْصُرُنْ اُنْصُرِنْ، وَكَذَلِكَ النَّهْيُ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ وَالْمَجْهُولِ.
text.en: You say with the heavy nūn: li-yanṣuranna li-yanṣurānni li-yanṣurunna li-tanṣuranna li-tanṣurānni li-yanṣurnānni, unṣuranna unṣurānni unṣurunna unṣurinna unṣurānni unṣurnānni; and with the light one: li-yanṣuran, with fatḥa on the rāʾ in the masculine singular; li-yanṣurun, with ḍamma on it in the masculine plural; li-tanṣuran, with fatḥa on the rāʾ in the feminine singular absent; and for the one addressed: unṣuran unṣurun unṣurin. The prohibition, active and passive, is likewise.

lessons.title: The participles in full; the four-letter verb
body: The participles of naṣara are given in full, and the book spells out the vowels of the less obvious words: nuṣṣār and nuṣṣar “with ḍamma on the nūn, fatḥa on the ṣād and doubling in both”, and naṣara “with fatḥa on the nūn, the ṣād and the rāʾ, without doubling”; manāṣir “with fatḥa on the mīm and kasra on the ṣād”. Spelling the vowels out in words is the old way of guarding them, before the vowel signs could be trusted in every copy.

Then the bare four-letter verb in the recital of the varied forms: daḥraja, yudaḥriju, daḥrajatan, diḥrājan, fa-huwa mudaḥrijun wa-dhāka mudaḥrajun; the command daḥrij, the prohibition lā tudaḥrij. Again the vowels are spelled out: yudaḥriju “with ḍamma on the yāʾ, kasra on the rāʾ and sukūn on the ḥāʾ”, the command “with fatḥa on the dāl and kasra on the rāʾ”. “And so is the conjugation of the attached forms”: ḥawqala, yuḥawqilu, ḥawqalatan, fa-huwa muḥawqilun, and the rest.

Notice the command daḥrij has no hamza: the dāl after the prefix of tudaḥriju has a vowel (lesson 8). And the participles are made by the rule of lesson 5: the passive present yudaḥraju with mu- gives mudaḥraj, the active with kasra mudaḥrij.
The recital of daḥraja is the model for every four-letter verb, sound or attached; the conjugation tool, which works with three-letter roots, does not give it.

terms.en: the model of the bare four-letter verb: daḥraja

tasks.answer: With fatḥa on the mīm and kasra on the ṣād (bi-fatḥ al-mīm wa-kasr al-ṣād).

quiz.explanation: Bi-ḍamm al-nūn wa-fatḥ al-ṣād …

quiz.prompt: What is the active participle of daḥraja?

text.original: مِثَالُ الْفَاعِلِ: نَاصِرٌ نَاصِرَانِ نَاصِرُونَ نُصَّارٌ وَنُصَّرٌ بِضَمِّ النُّونِ وَفَتْحِ الصَّادِ وَالتَّشْدِيدِ فِيهِمَا، وَنَصَرَةٌ بِفَتْحِ النُّونِ وَالصَّادِ وَالرَّاءِ مَعَ التَّخْفِيفِ، نَاصِرَةٌ نَاصِرَتَانِ نَاصِرَاتٌ وَنَوَاصِرُ. مِثَالُ الْمَفْعُولِ: مَنْصُورٌ مَنْصُورَانِ مَنْصُورُونَ وَمَنَاصِرُ بِفَتْحِ الْمِيمِ وَكَسْرِ الصَّادِ، مَنْصُورَةٌ مَنْصُورَتَانِ مَنْصُورَاتٌ.
text.en: Example of the active participle: nāṣirun nāṣirāni nāṣirūna nuṣṣārun wa-nuṣṣarun, with ḍamma on the nūn, fatḥa on the ṣād and doubling in both, wa-naṣaratun, with fatḥa on the nūn, the ṣād and the rāʾ, without doubling, nāṣiratun nāṣiratāni nāṣirātun wa-nawāṣiru. Example of the passive participle: manṣūrun manṣūrāni manṣūrūna wa-manāṣiru, with fatḥa on the mīm and kasra on the ṣād, manṣūratun manṣūratāni manṣūrātun.

text.original: مِثَالُ الرُّبَاعِيِّ الْمُجَرَّدِ: دَحْرَجَ يُدَحْرِجُ بِضَمِّ الْيَاءِ وَكَسْرِ الرَّاءِ وَسُكُونِ الْحَاءِ، دَحْرَجَةً بِفَتْحِ الدَّالِ وَسُكُونِ الْحَاءِ، وَدِحْرَاجًا بِكَسْرِ الدَّالِ وَسُكُونِ الْحَاءِ، فَهُوَ مُدَحْرِجٌ وَذَاكَ مُدَحْرَجٌ، وَالْأَمْرُ دَحْرِجْ بِفَتْحِ الدَّالِ وَكَسْرِ الرَّاءِ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تُدَحْرِجْ بِضَمِّ التَّاءِ وَكَسْرِ الرَّاءِ. وَكَذَلِكَ تَصْرِيفُ الْمُلْحَقَاتِ.
text.en: Example of the bare quadriliteral: daḥraja yudaḥriju “to roll”, with ḍamma on the yāʾ, kasra on the rāʾ and sukūn on the ḥāʾ; daḥrajatan, with fatḥa on the dāl and sukūn on the ḥāʾ, and wa-diḥrājan, with kasra on the dāl and sukūn on the ḥāʾ; fa-huwa mudaḥrijun wa-dhāka mudaḥrajun “so he is one who rolls, and that is rolled”; the imperative daḥrij, with fatḥa on the dāl and kasra on the rāʾ; and the prohibition lā tudaḥrij, with ḍamma on the tāʾ and kasra on the rāʾ. The conjugation of the attached forms is likewise.

lessons.title: The four-letter augmented forms: akhraja, kharraja, khāṣama
body: The augmented forms with a four-letter past are recited on new models: akhraja (afʿala), kharraja (faʿʿala), khāṣama (fāʿala). Akhraja, yukhriju, ikhrājan, fa-huwa mukhrijun wa-dhāka mukhrajun; the command akhrij, the prohibition lā tukhrij.

Then the book explains a form the student takes for granted. Why is the present yukhriju and not yuʾakhriju, with the hamza of afʿala? “The hamza was dropped from the present of this bāb so that two hamzas would not meet in the speaker's form”: the “I” form would be uʾakhriju, a hamza on a hamza. “And it was dropped also from the active and passive participles, the command to the absent and the prohibition, to keep the bāb regular (iṭṭirādan li-l-bāb).” One reason for one form, and regularity for the rest.

Kharraja, yukharriju, takhrījan and takhrijatan, “with kasra on the rāʾ and fatḥa on the tāʾ in both”, fa-huwa mukharrijun wa-dhāka mukharrajun; the command kharrij. Khāṣama, yukhāṣimu, mukhāṣamatan and khiṣāman, fa-huwa mukhāṣimun wa-dhāka mukhāṣamun; the command khāṣim. And its passive: khūṣima, “with ḍamma on the khāʾ”, in which the alif of fāʿala turns into a wāw after the ḍamma, and yukhāṣamu.
All three are regular, and the conjugation tool gives them as patterns 4, 2 and 3 for any sound root. Khūṣima shows a rule the weak verbs will need: a long ā after a ḍamma becomes ū.

tasks.prompt: Why is the present of akhraja yukhriju and not yuʾakhriju?
tasks.answer: The hamza of afʿala was dropped in the present so that two hamzas would not meet in the speaker's form (uʾakhriju). It was then dropped in all the other forms of the present and in the participles to keep the bāb regular.

tasks.prompt: Recite kātaba (fāʿala of kataba) and ʿallama (faʿʿala of ʿalima) as the book recites khāṣama and kharraja, with the conjugation tool's forms.

tasks.prompt: What happens to the alif of khāṣama in the passive past?
tasks.answer: The first letter takes a ḍamma (passive), and the long ā after it turns into ū, written with a wāw: khūṣima.

quiz.prompt: Why was the hamza of afʿala dropped in the present?
options: So that two hamzas would not meet in the speaker's form
Because it is a hamza of joining
quiz.explanation: Uʾakhriju would have two hamzas.

quiz.prompt: Why is it dropped in the other forms too?
options: Because they also have two hamzas
quiz.explanation: It was dropped in the present so that two hamzas would not meet in the speaker's form, and in the other forms to keep the bāb regular.

quiz.prompt: Which are the two maṣdars of kharraja in the book?
quiz.explanation: With kasra on the rāʾ and fatḥa on the tāʾ.

quiz.prompt: The passive past of khāṣama is…
quiz.explanation: The alif becomes wāw after the ḍamma.

quiz.prompt: The command of akhraja is…
quiz.explanation: Its hamza is always said.

quiz.prompt: What are the two maṣdars of khāṣama?
quiz.explanation: As qātala has muqātala and qitāl.

quiz.prompt: Which pattern is kharraja?
quiz.explanation: Kharraja doubles the ʿayn of kharaja: it is on faʿʿala.

text.original: مِثَالُ الرُّبَاعِيِّ الْمَزِيدِ فِيهِ: أَخْرَجَ يُخْرِجُ إِخْرَاجًا فَهُوَ مُخْرِجٌ وَذَاكَ مُخْرَجٌ، وَالْأَمْرُ أَخْرِجْ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تُخْرِجْ بِضَمِّ التَّاءِ وَكَسْرِ الرَّاءِ فِيهِمَا. وَقَدْ حُذِفَتِ الْهَمْزَةُ مِنْ مُسْتَقْبَلِ هَذَا الْبَابِ لِئَلَّا يَجْتَمِعَ هَمْزَتَانِ فِي نَفْسِ الْمُتَكَلِّمِ، وَكَذَلِكَ حُذِفَ مِنَ الْفَاعِلِ وَالْمَفْعُولِ وَأَمْرِ الْغَائِبِ وَالنَّهْيِ اطِّرَادًا لِلْبَابِ.
text.en: Example of the augmented four-letter verb: akhraja yukhriju ikhrājan fa-huwa mukhrijun wa-dhāka mukhrajun “to bring out”; the imperative akhrij; and the prohibition lā tukhrij, with ḍamma on the tāʾ and kasra on the rāʾ in both. The hamza has been dropped from the future of this bāb, so that two hamzas do not meet in the first person singular; and it has likewise been dropped from the active and passive participles, the command to the absent and the prohibition, to keep the bāb regular.

text.original: وَخَرَّجَ يُخَرِّجُ تَخْرِيجًا وَتَخْرِجَةً بِكَسْرِ الرَّاءِ وَفَتْحِ التَّاءِ فِيهِمَا، فَهُوَ مُخَرِّجٌ وَذَاكَ مُخَرَّجٌ، وَالْأَمْرُ خَرِّجْ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تُخَرِّجْ بِضَمِّ التَّاءِ وَكَسْرِ الرَّاءِ فِيهِمَا.
text.en: And kharraja yukharriju takhrījan wa-takhrijatan “to bring out, to train”, with kasra on the rāʾ and fatḥa on the tāʾ in both; fa-huwa mukharrijun wa-dhāka mukharrajun; the imperative kharrij; and the prohibition lā tukharrij, with ḍamma on the tāʾ and kasra on the rāʾ in both.

text.original: وَخَاصَمَ يُخَاصِمُ بِكَسْرِ الصَّادِ مُخَاصَمَةً بِفَتْحِ الصَّادِ وَخِصَامًا بِكَسْرِ الْخَاءِ، فَهُوَ مُخَاصِمٌ وَذَاكَ مُخَاصَمٌ، وَالْأَمْرُ خَاصِمْ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تُخَاصِمْ، وَمَجْهُولُ الْمَاضِي خُوصِمَ بِضَمِّ الْخَاءِ، وَمَجْهُولُ الْمُضَارِعِ يُخَاصَمُ بِفَتْحِ الصَّادِ.
text.en: And khāṣama yukhāṣimu “to dispute with”, with kasra on the ṣād, mukhāṣamatan, with fatḥa on the ṣād, and wa-khiṣāman, with kasra on the khāʾ; fa-huwa mukhāṣimun wa-dhāka mukhāṣamun; the imperative khāṣim; the prohibition lā tukhāṣim; the passive past khūṣima, with ḍamma on the khāʾ; and the passive muḍāriʿ yukhāṣamu, with fatḥa on the ṣād.

lessons.title: The five-letter forms
body: The five-letter forms are recited one by one, with the vowel of the letter before the last spelled out, for that is where they differ. Inkasara, yankasiru “with kasra on the sīn”, inkisāran, munkasir, inkasir, lā tankasir. Iktasaba, yaktasibu, iktisāban, muktasib and muktasab. Iṣfarra, “to turn yellow”, yaṣfarru “with fatḥa on the fāʾ”, iṣfirāran, muṣfarr; the command iṣfarra, the prohibition lā taṣfarra. Takassara, yatakassaru “with fatḥa on the sīn”, takassuran “with ḍamma on the sīn”, mutakassir “with kasra on the sīn”. Taṣālaḥa, yataṣālaḥu, taṣāluḥan, mutaṣāliḥ and mutaṣālaḥ.

The rule behind the list: in infaʿala and iftaʿala the letter before the last has a kasra in the present, the participle and the command; in tafaʿʿala and tafāʿala it has a fatḥa in the present and the command, a ḍamma in the maṣdar, a kasra in the active participle. Learn it once on these models and every verb of the five bābs follows.

Then two forms that look strange: iddaththara and iththāqala. “The base of the first is tadaththara, and of the second tathāqala, like taṣālaḥa; the tāʾ was assimilated into what follows it, then a hamza of joining was brought in so that one could begin with it, because one cannot begin with a quiescent letter.” The Qurʾān has both: yā ayyuhā al-muddaththiru, “O you wrapped in your cloak” (Q 74:1), the active participle of iddaththara; and mā lakum idhā qīla lakumu nfirū fī sabīli llāhi ththāqaltum ilā al-arḍi, “what is with you that, when you are told to go forth in God's way, you cling heavily to the earth?” (Q 9:38).

And the augmented four-letter verb tadaḥraja: yatadaḥraju “with fatḥa on the rāʾ”, tadaḥrujan “with ḍamma on the rāʾ”, mutadaḥrij “with kasra on the rāʾ”, the command tadaḥraj. It follows tafaʿʿala exactly, as its form suggests.

terms.en: the five-letter verbs: infaʿala, iftaʿala, ifʿalla, tafaʿʿala, tafāʿala
assimilation of the tāʾ: tadaththara → iddaththara
one cannot begin with a quiescent letter

takassara: fatḥa in the present, ḍamma in the maṣdar

tasks.prompt: Explain step by step how tadaththara becomes iddaththara.
tasks.answer: The tāʾ of tafaʿʿala is assimilated into the dāl after it: the two become a doubled dāl, and the word now begins with a quiescent letter. Since one cannot begin with a quiescent letter, a hamza of joining is brought in: iddaththara.

tasks.prompt: Give the vowel of the letter before the last in the present, the maṣdar and the active participle of takassara and taṣālaḥa.
tasks.answer: Takassara: fatḥa in the present (yatakassaru), ḍamma in the maṣdar (takassur), kasra in the participle (mutakassir). Taṣālaḥa: fatḥa (yataṣālaḥu), ḍamma (taṣāluḥ), kasra (mutaṣāliḥ).

tasks.prompt: Recite inqaṭaʿa and intaqala (from the conjugation tool) in the order of the book: past, present, maṣdar, active participle, command.
tasks.answer: Inqaṭaʿa, yanqaṭiʿu, inqiṭāʿ, munqaṭiʿ, inqaṭiʿ. Intaqala, yantaqilu, intiqāl, muntaqil, intaqil.

tasks.prompt: Find the participle of iddaththara in Q 74:1 and give its pattern.
tasks.answer: Al-muddaththir, “the one wrapped in a cloak”: the active participle of iddaththara (from tadaththara, tafaʿʿala), with mu- and a kasra before the last letter.

quiz.prompt: The present of inkasara has which vowel on the sīn?
quiz.explanation: Infaʿala and iftaʿala: kasra before the last letter.

quiz.prompt: The maṣdar of takassara has which vowel on the sīn?
quiz.explanation: Takassara is tafaʿʿala, whose maṣdar is tafaʿʿul with a ḍamma on the ʿayn: takassur.

quiz.prompt: What is the base of iththāqala?
quiz.explanation: The tāʾ assimilated, then a hamza of joining.

quiz.prompt: Why is a hamza of joining added in iddaththara?
options: One cannot begin with a quiescent letter
quiz.explanation: After assimilation the word begins with a doubled, quiescent dāl.

quiz.prompt: Al-muddaththir in Q 74:1 is…
quiz.explanation: “The one wrapped in his cloak.”

quiz.prompt: The command of iṣfarra is…
quiz.explanation: The doubled end keeps its fatḥa.

quiz.prompt: Which five-letter form follows tadaḥraja's pattern of vowels?
quiz.explanation: Fatḥa in the present, ḍamma in the maṣdar, kasra in the participle.

text.original: مِثَالُ الْخُمَاسِيِّ: انْكَسَرَ يَنْكَسِرُ بِكَسْرِ السِّينِ انْكِسَارًا فَهُوَ مُنْكَسِرٌ، وَالْأَمْرُ انْكَسِرْ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تَنْكَسِرْ، بِكَسْرِ السِّينِ فِي الثَّلَاثِ. وَاكْتَسَبَ يَكْتَسِبُ اكْتِسَابًا فَهُوَ مُكْتَسِبٌ وَذَاكَ مُكْتَسَبٌ، وَالْأَمْرُ اكْتَسِبْ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تَكْتَسِبْ، بِكَسْرِ السِّينِ فِيهِمَا.
text.en: Example of the five-letter verb: inkasara yankasiru “to be broken”, with kasra on the sīn, inkisāran fa-huwa munkasirun; the imperative inkasir; and the prohibition lā tankasir, with kasra on the sīn in the three. And iktasaba yaktasibu iktisāban fa-huwa muktasibun wa-dhāka muktasabun “to earn”; the imperative iktasib; and the prohibition lā taktasib, with kasra on the sīn in both.

text.original: وَاصْفَرَّ يَصْفَرُّ بِفَتْحِ الْفَاءِ فِيهِمَا اصْفِرَارًا فَهُوَ مُصْفَرٌّ بِفَتْحِ الْفَاءِ، وَالْأَمْرُ اصْفَرَّ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تَصْفَرَّ، بِفَتْحِ الْفَاءِ فِيهِمَا. وَتَكَسَّرَ يَتَكَسَّرُ بِفَتْحِ السِّينِ فِيهِمَا تَكَسُّرًا بِضَمِّ السِّينِ فَهُوَ مُتَكَسِّرٌ بِكَسْرِ السِّينِ، وَالْأَمْرُ تَكَسَّرْ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تَتَكَسَّرْ، بِفَتْحِ السِّينِ فِيهِمَا.
text.en: And iṣfarra yaṣfarru “to turn yellow”, with fatḥa on the fāʾ in both, iṣfirāran fa-huwa muṣfarrun, with fatḥa on the fāʾ; the imperative iṣfarra; and the prohibition lā taṣfarra, with fatḥa on the fāʾ in both. And takassara yatakassaru “to break into pieces”, with fatḥa on the sīn in both, takassuran, with ḍamma on the sīn, fa-huwa mutakassirun, with kasra on the sīn; the imperative takassar; and the prohibition lā tatakassar, with fatḥa on the sīn in both.

text.original: وَتَصَالَحَ يَتَصَالَحُ بِفَتْحِ اللَّامِ فِيهِمَا تَصَالُحًا بِضَمِّ اللَّامِ فَهُوَ مُتَصَالِحٌ بِكَسْرِ اللَّامِ وَذَاكَ مُتَصَالَحٌ بِفَتْحِ اللَّامِ، وَالْأَمْرُ تَصَالَحْ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تَتَصَالَحْ، بِفَتْحِ اللَّامِ فِيهِمَا.
text.en: And taṣālaḥa yataṣālaḥu “to make peace with one another”, with fatḥa on the lām in both, taṣāluḥan, with ḍamma on the lām, fa-huwa mutaṣāliḥun, with kasra on the lām, wa-dhāka mutaṣālaḥun, with fatḥa on the lām; the imperative taṣālaḥ; and the prohibition lā tataṣālaḥ, with fatḥa on the lām in both.

text.original: وَأَمَّا ادَّثَّرَ وَاثَّاقَلَ فَأَصْلُ الْأَوَّلِ تَدَثَّرَ، وَأَصْلُ الثَّانِي تَثَاقَلَ كَتَصَالَحَ، فَأُدْغِمَتِ التَّاءُ فِيمَا بَعْدَهَا، ثُمَّ أُدْخِلَتْ هَمْزَةُ الْوَصْلِ لِيُمْكِنَ الِابْتِدَاءُ بِهَا؛ لِأَنَّ السَّاكِنَ لَا يُبْتَدَأُ بِهِ. وَتَصْرِيفُهُ: ادَّثَّرَ يَدَّثَّرُ بِفَتْحِ الثَّاءِ فِيهِمَا ادِّثُّرًا بِضَمِّ الثَّاءِ فَهُوَ مُدَّثِّرٌ بِكَسْرِ الثَّاءِ، وَالْأَمْرُ ادَّثَّرْ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تَدَّثَّرْ، بِفَتْحِ الثَّاءِ فِيهِمَا، وَبِفَتْحِ الدَّالِ وَالتَّشْدِيدِ فِي الْجَمِيعِ.
text.en: As for iddaththara and iththāqala, the origin of the first is tadaththara and the origin of the second tathāqala, like taṣālaḥa; the tāʾ was assimilated into what follows it, and then the hamza of connection was brought in so that one could begin with it, for one does not begin with an unvowelled letter. Its conjugation: iddaththara yaddaththaru “to wrap oneself up”, with fatḥa on the thāʾ in both, iddiththuran, with ḍamma on the thāʾ, fa-huwa muddaththirun, with kasra on the thāʾ; the imperative iddaththar; and the prohibition lā taddaththar, with fatḥa on the thāʾ in both, and with fatḥa and doubling on the dāl in all.

text.original: وَاثَّاقَلَ يَثَّاقَلُ اثِّاقُلًا بِضَمِّ الْقَافِ فَهُوَ مُثَّاقِلٌ بِكَسْرِ الْقَافِ وَذَاكَ مُثَّاقَلٌ بِفَتْحِ الْقَافِ، وَالْأَمْرُ اثَّاقَلْ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تَثَّاقَلْ، بِفَتْحِ الْقَافِ فِيهِمَا، وَالثَّاءُ مُشَدَّدَةٌ فِي الْجَمِيعِ.
text.en: And iththāqala yaththāqalu iththiqulan “to be sluggish”, with ḍamma on the qāf, fa-huwa muththāqilun, with kasra on the qāf, wa-dhāka muththāqalun, with fatḥa on the qāf; the imperative iththāqal; and the prohibition lā taththāqal, with fatḥa on the qāf in both; and the thāʾ is doubled in all.

text.original: وَتَدَحْرَجَ يَتَدَحْرَجُ بِفَتْحِ الرَّاءِ فِيهِمَا تَدَحْرُجًا بِضَمِّ الرَّاءِ فَهُوَ مُتَدَحْرِجٌ بِكَسْرِ الرَّاءِ، وَالْأَمْرُ تَدَحْرَجْ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تَتَدَحْرَجْ، بِفَتْحِ الرَّاءِ فِيهِمَا.
text.en: And tadaḥraja yatadaḥraju “to roll [of itself]”, with fatḥa on the rāʾ in both, tadaḥrujan, with ḍamma on the rāʾ, fa-huwa mutadaḥrijun, with kasra on the rāʾ; the imperative tadaḥraj; and the prohibition lā tatadaḥraj, with fatḥa on the rāʾ in both.

lessons.title: The six-letter forms
body: The six-letter forms, in the same way. Istaghfara, yastaghfiru “with kasra on the fāʾ”, istighfāran, mustaghfir “with kasra on the fāʾ” and mustaghfar “with fatḥa”, istaghfir, lā tastaghfir. Ishhābba, “to turn grey”, yashhābbu, ishhībāban, mushhābb, ishhābba, lā tashhābba, “with the bāʾ doubled everywhere except in the maṣdar”.

Ighdawdana, “to grow long and thick” (of hair), yaghdawdinu “with kasra on the second dāl”, ighdīdānan, mughdawdin, ighdawdin. Ijlawwadha, yajlawwidhu “with kasra on the wāw”, ijliwwādhan, mujlawwidh, ijlawwidh, “and the wāw is doubled everywhere”. Isḥankaka, “to be pitch dark”, yasḥankiku “with kasra on the first kāf”, isḥinkākan, musḥankik. Islanqā, yaslanqī, islinqāʾan, muslanqin; the command islanqi, the prohibition lā taslanqi, its weak end dropped.

And the augmented four-letter verbs: iqshaʿarra, yaqshaʿirru “with kasra on the ʿayn”, iqshiʿrāran, muqshaʿirr, iqshaʿirra, “and the rāʾ doubled everywhere except in the maṣdar”; iḥranjama, yaḥranjimu “with kasra on the jīm”, iḥrinjāman, muḥranjim, iḥranjim.

Two things to see. In every six-letter verb the letter before the last has a kasra in the present, the participle and the command, as the rule of lesson 7 said. And in the maṣdar a doubled letter is undone and a long ī appears: ishhābba, ishhībāb; iqshaʿarra, iqshiʿrār. The conjugation tool gives only istafʿala of these; the others are recited from the print.

terms.en: the six-letter verbs
except in the maṣdar, where the doubling is undone
with kasra on the ʿayn: the vowel before the last letter

islanqā: a weak end; the participle muslanqin

tasks.prompt: Recite istakhraja from the conjugation tool in the book's order, with both participles.
tasks.answer: Istakhraja, yastakhriju, istikhrājan, fa-huwa mustakhrijun wa-dhāka mustakhrajun; istakhrij, lā tastakhrij.

tasks.prompt: What happens to the doubled letter of ishhābba and iqshaʿarra in the maṣdar?
tasks.answer: The doubling is undone: ishhībāb (with a long ī and two separate bāʾs) and iqshiʿrār (two separate rāʾs). Everywhere else the letter stays doubled.

tasks.prompt: Which vowel does the letter before the last take in the present of every six-letter verb? Show it on three.
tasks.answer: A kasra: yastaghfiru (fāʾ), yaghdawdinu (second dāl), yaḥranjimu (jīm).

quiz.prompt: In yastaghfiru, the fāʾ has…
quiz.explanation: The letter before the last in the present of the six-letter verbs.

quiz.prompt: What does ishhābba mean?
quiz.explanation: Ishhābba is on ifʿālla, from shuhba, greyness: to turn grey.

quiz.prompt: Where is the bāʾ of ishhābba not doubled?
quiz.explanation: In the maṣdar ishhībāb the long ī stands between the two bāʾs, so they cannot be assimilated.

quiz.prompt: Isḥankaka means…
quiz.explanation: Ifʿanlala, with the lām repeated.

quiz.prompt: The active participle of islanqā is…
quiz.explanation: Its weak end drops before the tanwīn.

quiz.prompt: Which of these six-letter forms does the conjugation tool give?
quiz.explanation: The others are recited from the print.

quiz.prompt: The command of iḥranjama is…
quiz.explanation: With kasra on the jīm.

text.original: مِثَالُ السُّدَاسِيِّ: اسْتَغْفَرَ يَسْتَغْفِرُ بِكَسْرِ الْفَاءِ اسْتِغْفَارًا فَهُوَ مُسْتَغْفِرٌ بِكَسْرِ الْفَاءِ وَذَاكَ مُسْتَغْفَرٌ بِفَتْحِ الْفَاءِ، وَالْأَمْرُ اسْتَغْفِرْ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تَسْتَغْفِرْ، بِكَسْرِ الْفَاءِ فِيهِمَا. وَاشْهَابَّ يَشْهَابُّ اشْهِيبَابًا فَهُوَ مُشْهَابٌّ، وَالْأَمْرُ اشْهَابَّ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تَشْهَابَّ، بِتَشْدِيدِ الْبَاءِ فِي الْجَمِيعِ إِلَّا فِي الْمَصْدَرِ.
text.en: Example of the six-letter verb: istaghfara yastaghfiru “to ask forgiveness”, with kasra on the fāʾ, istighfāran fa-huwa mustaghfirun, with kasra on the fāʾ, wa-dhāka mustaghfarun, with fatḥa on the fāʾ; the imperative istaghfir; and the prohibition lā tastaghfir, with kasra on the fāʾ in both. And ishhābba yashhābbu ishhībāban fa-huwa mushhābbun “to turn grey”; the imperative ishhābba; and the prohibition lā tashhābba, with doubling of the bāʾ in all except the maṣdar.

text.original: وَاغْدَوْدَنَ يَغْدَوْدِنُ بِكَسْرِ الدَّالِ الثَّانِيَةِ اغْدِيدَانًا فَهُوَ مُغْدَوْدِنٌ، وَالْأَمْرُ اغْدَوْدِنْ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تَغْدَوْدِنْ، بِكَسْرِ الدَّالِ الثَّانِيَةِ فِي الثَّلَاثِ. وَاجْلَوَّذَ يَجْلَوِّذُ بِكَسْرِ الْوَاوِ اجْلِوَّاذًا فَهُوَ مُجْلَوِّذٌ، وَالْأَمْرُ اجْلَوِّذْ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تَجْلَوِّذْ، بِكَسْرِ الْوَاوِ فِي الثَّلَاثِ، وَالْوَاوُ مُشَدَّدَةٌ فِي الْجَمِيعِ.
text.en: And ighdawdana yaghdawdinu “to grow long and thick [of hair]”, with kasra on the second dāl, ighdīdānan fa-huwa mughdawdinun; the imperative ighdawdin; and the prohibition lā taghdawdin, with kasra on the second dāl in the three. And ijlawwadha yajlawwidhu “to press on fast”, with kasra on the wāw, ijliwwādhan fa-huwa mujlawwidhun; the imperative ijlawwidh; and the prohibition lā tajlawwidh, with kasra on the wāw in the three; and the wāw is doubled in all.

text.original: وَاسْحَنْكَكَ يَسْحَنْكِكُ بِكَسْرِ الْكَافِ الْأُولَى اسْحِنْكَاكًا فَهُوَ مُسْحَنْكِكٌ، وَالْأَمْرُ اسْحَنْكِكْ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تَسْحَنْكِكْ، بِكَسْرِ الْكَافِ فِي الثَّلَاثِ. وَاسْلَنْقَى يَسْلَنْقِي اسْلِنْقَاءً فَهُوَ مُسْلَنْقٍ، وَالْأَمْرُ اسْلَنْقِ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تَسْلَنْقِ، بِكَسْرِ الْقَافِ فِيهِمَا.
text.en: And isḥankaka yasḥankiku “to be pitch dark”, with kasra on the first kāf, isḥinkākan fa-huwa musḥankikun; the imperative isḥankik; and the prohibition lā tasḥankik, with kasra on the kāf in the three. And islanqā yaslanqī islinqāʾan fa-huwa muslanqin “to fall on one's back”; the imperative islanqi; and the prohibition lā taslanqi, with kasra on the qāf in both.

text.original: وَاقْشَعَرَّ يَقْشَعِرُّ بِكَسْرِ الْعَيْنِ اقْشِعْرَارًا فَهُوَ مُقْشَعِرٌّ، وَالْأَمْرُ اقْشَعِرَّ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تَقْشَعِرَّ، بِكَسْرِ الْعَيْنِ فِي الثَّلَاثِ، وَالرَّاءُ مُشَدَّدَةٌ فِي الْجَمِيعِ إِلَّا فِي الْمَصْدَرِ. وَاحْرَنْجَمَ يَحْرَنْجِمُ بِكَسْرِ الْجِيمِ احْرِنْجَامًا فَهُوَ مُحْرَنْجِمٌ، وَالْأَمْرُ احْرَنْجِمْ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تَحْرَنْجِمْ، بِكَسْرِ الْجِيمِ فِي الثَّلَاثِ.
text.en: And iqshaʿarra yaqshaʿirru “to shudder”, with kasra on the ʿayn, iqshiʿrāran fa-huwa muqshaʿirrun; the imperative iqshaʿirra; and the prohibition lā taqshaʿirra, with kasra on the ʿayn in the three; and the rāʾ is doubled in all except the maṣdar. And iḥranjama yaḥranjimu “to crowd together”, with kasra on the jīm, iḥrinjāman fa-huwa muḥranjimun; the imperative iḥranjim; and the prohibition lā taḥranjim, with kasra on the jīm in the three.

lessons.title: Making a verb transitive or intransitive
body: The section of useful points (fawāʾid) begins with transitivity. An intransitive verb becomes transitive “by one of three causes”: a hamza added at its start, akhrajtuhu, “I brought him out”; its ʿayn doubled, kharrajtuhu; or a particle of jarr after it, kharajtu bihi min al-dāri, “I went out with him from the house”, that is, took him out. And also by dropping the tāʾ from tafaʿʿala and tafaʿlala: taʿallama, “to learn”, becomes ʿallama, “to teach”; tadaḥraja becomes daḥraja.

The reverse: a transitive verb becomes intransitive by removing the causes of transitivity, or by moving it to the bāb of inkasara (kasara → inkasara), and faʿlala becomes intransitive by adding a tāʾ at its start (daḥraja → tadaḥraja). Compliance, the Binā's muṭāwaʿa, is one of the ways a verb loses its object.

Then a rule with a consequence for naḥw: “the object and the passive do not come from the intransitive, because the intransitive verb is the one that needs no object, and the transitive is the opposite”. So kharaja has no passive participle with the sense “taken out”, and no passive past in the fourteen persons; to say that, Arabic uses akhraja, ukhrija, mukhraj.

Taken together, the three causes are the ṣarf behind what the ʿAwāmil and the Ājurrūmiyya call the object. A particle of jarr makes a verb reach a noun (kharajtu bihi); the hamza and the doubling make it reach the noun directly (akhrajtuhu, kharrajtuhu).

terms.en: the causes of transitivity: hamza, doubling, a particle
the intransitive verb
the transitive verb
no passive from the intransitive

examples.arabic: أَخْرَجْتُهُ، وَخَرَّجْتُهُ، وَخَرَجْتُ بِهِ مِنَ الدَّارِ
examples.en: three ways to make kharaja transitive: hamza, doubling, a particle
taʿallama, “to learn”, becomes ʿallama, “to teach”, by dropping the tāʾ
kasara, “to break”, becomes inkasara, “to break (intransitive)”: moved to the bāb of inkasara

tasks.prompt: Make jalasa, “to sit”, transitive in two ways with the conjugation tool's forms, and translate.
tasks.answer: Ajlasa (afʿala), “to seat someone”: ajlastu Zaydan, “I seated Zayd”; and with a particle, jalasa bi- or ilā, as jalastu ilā Zaydin, “I sat with Zayd”.

tasks.prompt: Why does kharaja have no passive in the fourteen persons, according to the Maqṣūd?
tasks.answer: Because it is intransitive: the intransitive verb needs no object, and the passive and the passive participle come only from a verb with an object. To say “he was brought out”, Arabic uses the transitive akhraja: ukhrija.

tasks.prompt: Name the change in each pair: kasara → inkasara; taʿallama → ʿallama; daḥraja → tadaḥraja.
tasks.answer: Kasara → inkasara: transitive to intransitive by moving to the bāb of inkasara. Taʿallama → ʿallama: intransitive to transitive by dropping the tāʾ. Daḥraja → tadaḥraja: transitive to intransitive by adding a tāʾ to faʿlala.

quiz.prompt: How many causes make an intransitive verb transitive, in the book?
quiz.explanation: And also dropping the tāʾ of tafaʿʿala and tafaʿlala.

quiz.prompt: Kharajtu bihi min al-dāri uses which cause?
quiz.explanation: Bi- makes the verb reach a noun.

quiz.prompt: How does taʿallama become transitive?
quiz.explanation: “To learn” becomes “to teach”.

quiz.prompt: How does daḥraja become intransitive?
quiz.explanation: Tafaʿlala is its compliance.

quiz.prompt: Which forms do not come from the intransitive?
options: The passive and the passive participle
quiz.explanation: The passive and the passive participle need an object, so an intransitive verb does not give them.

quiz.prompt: Kasara → inkasara changes the verb…
quiz.explanation: By moving it to the bāb of inkasara.

quiz.prompt: Akhrajtuhu means…
quiz.explanation: The hamza of afʿala made kharaja transitive.

text.original: اللَّازِمُ يَصِيرُ مُتَعَدِّيًا بِأَحَدِ ثَلَاثَةِ أَسْبَابٍ: بِزِيَادَةِ الْهَمْزَةِ فِي أَوَّلِهِ، وَحَرْفِ الْجَرِّ فِي آخِرِهِ، وَتَشْدِيدِ عَيْنِهِ، نَحْوُ: أَخْرَجْتُهُ، وَخَرَّجْتُهُ، وَخَرَجْتُ بِهِ مِنَ الدَّارِ، وَبِحَذْفِ التَّاءِ مِنْ تَفَعَّلَ وَتَفَعْلَلَ مُشَدَّدَةِ الْعَيْنِ وَمُكَرَّرَةِ اللَّامِ.
text.en: The intransitive becomes transitive by one of three means: the addition of the hamza at its beginning, a particle of jarr at its end, or the doubling of its ʿayn, as akhrajtuhu “I brought him out”, kharrajtuhu “I brought him out” and kharajtu bi-hi mina al-dāri “I went out with him from the house”; and by dropping the tāʾ from tafaʿʿala and tafaʿlala, with doubled ʿayn and repeated lām.

text.original: وَالْمُتَعَدِّي يَصِيرُ لَازِمًا بِحَذْفِ أَسْبَابِ التَّعْدِيَةِ، أَوْ بِنَقْلِهِ إِلَى بَابِ انْكَسَرَ، وَبَابُ فَعْلَلَ يَصِيرُ لَازِمًا بِزِيَادَةِ التَّاءِ فِي أَوَّلِهِ. وَلَا يَجِيءُ الْمَفْعُولُ بِهِ وَالْمَجْهُولُ مِنَ اللَّازِمِ؛ لِأَنَّ اللَّازِمَ مِنَ الْأَفْعَالِ هُوَ مَا لَا يَحْتَاجُ إِلَى الْمَفْعُولِ بِهِ، وَالْمُتَعَدِّي بِخِلَافِهِ.
text.en: The transitive becomes intransitive by dropping the means of transitivity, or by moving it to the bāb of inkasara; and the bāb of faʿlala becomes intransitive by adding the tāʾ at its beginning. The direct object and the passive do not come from the intransitive, for the intransitive among verbs is that which does not need a direct object, and the transitive is the opposite.

lessons.title: Sharing; the changes of iftaʿala; the letters of increase
lessons.arabic: الْمُشَارَكَةُ وَتَغْيِيرُ تَاءِ افْتَعَلَ وَحُرُوفُ الزِّيَادَةِ
lessons.transliteration: al-mushāraka wa-taghyīr tāʾ iftaʿala wa-ḥurūf al-ziyāda
body: Fāʿala is for sharing between two: nāḍaltuhu, “I vied with him in shooting”, “except in a few cases”: ṭāraqtu al-naʿla, “I sewed a second sole onto the sandal”, ʿāqabtu al-liṣṣa, “I punished the thief”, where only one person acts. Tafāʿala is for sharing between two or more: tadāfaʿnā, “we pushed one another”, taṣālaḥa al-qawmu, “the people made peace”; and it can show what is not within: tamāraḍtu, “I feigned illness”, that is, I showed illness and had none.

Then the tāʾ of iftaʿala, which changes beside some letters. If the fāʾ of the verb is one of the letters of covering (ḥurūf al-iṭbāq), ṣād, ḍād, ṭāʾ, ẓāʾ, the tāʾ becomes a ṭāʾ: iṣṭabara, iḍṭaraba, iṭṭarada, iẓẓahara. If the fāʾ is a dāl, a dhāl or a zāy, the tāʾ becomes a dāl: iddamaʿa, iddakara (with the dhāl assimilated into the dāl), izdajara. The heavy, “covered” letters pull the light tāʾ towards themselves.

If the fāʾ is a wāw, a yāʾ or a thāʾ, it turns into a tāʾ and is assimilated into the tāʾ of iftaʿala: ittaqā, “to guard oneself, fear God” (from w-q-y), ittasara, “to play at maysir” (from y-s-r), ittaghara, “to lose the milk teeth” (from th-gh-r). The familiar word taqwā and the verb ittaqā in the Qurʾān come from this change.

Last, the ten letters that are added in nouns and verbs, gathered in the phrase al-yawma tansāhu, “today you forget it”: hamza, lām, yāʾ, wāw, mīm, tāʾ, nūn, sīn, alif and hāʾ. Every added letter in the patterns of the Binā is one of them. A beginner can check each pattern: the hamza of afʿala, the sīn and tāʾ of istafʿala, the nūn of infaʿala, the mīm of mafʿal.

tasks.prompt: What would iftaʿala of ṣabara be by the plain pattern, and what does Arabic say? Explain.
tasks.answer: By the plain pattern it would be iṣtabara. Because the fāʾ is a ṣād, a letter of covering, the tāʾ becomes a ṭāʾ: iṣṭabara, “to be patient, persevere”.

tasks.prompt: From which roots do ittaqā and iddakara come, and what happened in each?
tasks.answer: Ittaqā is from w-q-y: the wāw turned into a tāʾ and was assimilated into the tāʾ of iftaʿala. Iddakara is from dh-k-r: the tāʾ became a dāl after the dhāl, and the dhāl was assimilated into the dāl.

tasks.prompt: Name the ten letters of increase and find the added letters of istakhraja and mukram among them.
tasks.answer: Al-yawma tansāhu: hamza, lām, yāʾ, wāw, mīm, tāʾ, nūn, sīn, alif, hāʾ. Istakhraja: the hamza, sīn and tāʾ. Mukram: the mīm.

tasks.prompt: Tamāraḍtu: what does tafāʿala add here, and how does it differ from taṣālaḥa al-qawmu?
tasks.answer: Tamāraḍtu means showing what is not within: “I feigned illness”. Taṣālaḥa al-qawmu is sharing: the people made peace with one another.

quiz.explanation: After a ṣād the tāʾ of iftaʿala becomes a ṭāʾ: iṣṭabara, not iṣtabara.

quiz.explanation: After a zāy the tāʾ of iftaʿala becomes a dāl: izdajara, not iztajara.

quiz.explanation: The wāw became a tāʾ and was assimilated.
