quiz.explanation: Hamza, lām, yāʾ, wāw, mīm, tāʾ, nūn, sīn, alif, hāʾ.

quiz.prompt: Which are the letters of covering (iṭbāq)?
quiz.explanation: They pull the tāʾ towards ṭāʾ.

text.original: وَبَابُ فَاعَلَ يَكُونُ لِلْمُشَارَكَةِ بَيْنَ الِاثْنَيْنِ، نَحْوُ: نَاضَلْتُهُ، إِلَّا قَلِيلًا، نَحْوُ: طَارَقْتُ النَّعْلَ، وَعَاقَبْتُ اللِّصَّ. وَبَابُ تَفَاعَلَ أَيْضًا يَكُونُ بَيْنَ الِاثْنَيْنِ فَصَاعِدًا، نَحْوُ: تَدَافَعْنَا، وَتَصَالَحَ الْقَوْمُ، وَيَكُونُ لِإِظْهَارِ مَا لَيْسَ فِي الْبَاطِنِ، نَحْوُ: تَمَارَضْتُ، أَيْ أَظْهَرْتُ الْمَرَضَ وَلَيْسَ بِي مَرَضٌ.
text.en: The bāb of fāʿala is for sharing between two, as nāḍaltuhu “I vied with him in shooting”, except in a few, as ṭāraqtu al-naʿla “I sewed a second sole onto the sandal” and ʿāqabtu al-liṣṣa “I punished the thief”. The bāb of tafāʿala is also between two and more, as tadāfaʿnā “we pushed one another” and taṣālaḥa al-qawmu “the people made peace with one another”; and it is for showing what is not within, as tamāraḍtu, that is, I showed sickness when there was no sickness in me.

text.original: وَإِذَا كَانَ فَاءُ الْفِعْلِ مِنِ افْتَعَلَ حَرْفًا مِنْ حُرُوفِ الْإِطْبَاقِ، وَهِيَ الصَّادُ وَالضَّادُ وَالطَّاءُ وَالظَّاءُ، يَصِيرُ تَاءُ افْتَعَلَ طَاءً، نَحْوُ: اصْطَبَرَ، وَاضْطَرَبَ، وَاطَّرَدَ، وَاظَّهَرَ. وَإِذَا كَانَ فَاءُ افْتَعَلَ دَالًا أَوْ ذَالًا أَوْ زَاءً يَصِيرُ تَاءُ افْتَعَلَ دَالًا، نَحْوُ: ادَّمَعَ، وَادَّكَرَ بِإِدْغَامِ الذَّالِ فِي الدَّالِ، وَازْدَجَرَ.
text.en: When the fāʾ of the verb of iftaʿala is one of the covered letters (ḥurūf al-iṭbāq), which are ṣād, ḍād, ṭāʾ and ẓāʾ, the tāʾ of iftaʿala becomes ṭāʾ, as iṣṭabara “to be patient”, iḍṭaraba “to be agitated”, iṭṭarada “to run on regularly” and iẓẓahara “to appear”. When the fāʾ of iftaʿala is dāl, dhāl or zāy, the tāʾ of iftaʿala becomes dāl, as iddamaʿa, iddakara “to remember”, with assimilation of the dhāl into the dāl, and izdajara “to be restrained”.

text.original: وَإِذَا كَانَ فَاؤُهُ وَاوًا أَوْ يَاءً أَوْ ثَاءً قُلِبَتِ الْوَاوُ وَالْيَاءُ وَالثَّاءُ تَاءً، ثُمَّ أُدْغِمَتْ فِي تَاءِ افْتَعَلَ، نَحْوُ: اتَّقَى، وَاتَّسَرَ، وَاتَّغَرَ. وَالْحُرُوفُ الَّتِي تُزَادُ فِي الْأَسْمَاءِ وَالْأَفْعَالِ عَشَرَةٌ، يَجْمَعُهَا: الْيَوْمَ تَنْسَاهُ.
text.en: When its fāʾ is wāw, yāʾ or thāʾ, the wāw, the yāʾ and the thāʾ are turned into tāʾ and then assimilated into the tāʾ of iftaʿala, as ittaqā “to be godfearing”, ittasara “to play at maysir” and ittaghara “to lose the milk teeth”. The letters that are added in nouns and verbs are ten, gathered in al-yawma tansāhu “today you forget it”.

lessons.title: How to judge an added letter; which bābs take an object
body: A practical rule: “if a word has more than three letters and one of these letters is in it, judge that it is added, unless the word has no meaning without it”, as in waswasa, whose wāws are root letters, since without them nothing is left. So in akrama the hamza is added (k-r-m means nobility without it), and in maktūb the mīm and the wāw; but in waswasa nothing is added.

Then a survey of the bābs. “The bābs of the four-letter past are all transitive, except darbakha.” The five-letter bābs are all intransitive except three, iftaʿala, tafaʿʿala and tafāʿala, which are shared between the two. The six-letter bābs are all intransitive except istafʿala, which is shared, and two words of ifʿanlā that are transitive: israndāhu and ighrandāhu, “he overcame him and subdued him”.

The survey is a beginner's guide, not a law without exceptions: the Binā gave aṣbaḥa al-rajulu as an intransitive afʿala, and the Maqṣūd itself will list it among the meanings of the hamza in the next lesson. Read “all” as “nearly all”, and expect the dictionary to have the last word.

What the survey does show is the shape of the system. The short augmented forms mostly add an object (akrama, ʿallama, qātala); the longer ones mostly take it away (inkasara, iḥmarra, iqshaʿarra). Adding letters to the front of a verb tends to turn its act back onto the doer.

tasks.prompt: Which letters are added in each: maktūb; istakhraja; waswasa; inkasara?
tasks.answer: Maktūb: the mīm and the wāw (root k-t-b). Istakhraja: the hamza, sīn and tāʾ (root kh-r-j). Waswasa: none; all four are root letters. Inkasara: the hamza and the nūn (root k-s-r).

tasks.prompt: Which five-letter bābs can be transitive? Give an example of one with an object, from the earlier lessons.
tasks.answer: Iftaʿala, tafaʿʿala and tafāʿala. Example: taʿallamtu al-ʿilma, “I learnt knowledge” (tafaʿʿala with an object).

tasks.prompt: Why should “all” in this survey be read as “nearly all”?
tasks.answer: Because there are known exceptions besides those the book names: the Binā gave aṣbaḥa al-rajulu, an intransitive afʿala, though the Maqṣūd calls the four-letter bābs transitive; and the Maqṣūd itself lists aṣbaḥa among the meanings of the hamza.

quiz.explanation: Istakhraja al-māla, istaḥjara al-ṭīnu.

quiz.explanation: Two transitive words of ifʿanlā.

quiz.explanation: Without them the word has no meaning.

text.original: فَإِذَا كَانَتْ كَلِمَةٌ وَعَدَدُهَا زَائِدٌ عَلَى ثَلَاثَةِ أَحْرُفٍ وَفِيهَا حَرْفٌ وَاحِدٌ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْحُرُوفِ فَاحْكُمْ بِأَنَّهَا زَائِدَةٌ، إِلَّا أَنْ لَا يَكُونَ لَهَا مَعْنًى بِدُونِهَا، نَحْوُ: وَسْوَسَ. وَأَبْوَابُ الرُّبَاعِيِّ كُلُّهَا مُتَعَدٍّ إِلَّا دَرْبَخَ، وَأَبْوَابُ الْخُمَاسِيِّ كُلُّهَا لَوَازِمُ إِلَّا ثَلَاثَةَ أَبْوَابٍ: افْتَعَلَ وَتَفَعَّلَ وَتَفَاعَلَ، فَإِنَّهَا مُشْتَرَكَةٌ بَيْنَ اللَّازِمِ وَالْمُتَعَدِّي.
text.en: So when a word has more than three letters and one of these letters is in it, judge that it is added, unless the word has no meaning without it, as waswasa “to whisper evil”. The bābs of the quadriliteral are all transitive except darbakha; and the bābs of the five-letter verb are all intransitive except three bābs, iftaʿala, tafaʿʿala and tafāʿala, which are shared between the intransitive and the transitive.

text.original: وَأَبْوَابُ السُّدَاسِيِّ كُلُّهَا لَوَازِمُ إِلَّا بَابَ اسْتَفْعَلَ فَإِنَّهُ مُشْتَرَكٌ بَيْنَ اللَّازِمِ وَالْمُتَعَدِّي، وَكَلِمَتَيْنِ مِنْ بَابِ افْعَنْلَى فَإِنَّهُمَا مُتَعَدِّيَانِ، وَهُمَا: اسْرَنْدَاهُ وَاغْرَنْدَاهُ، مَعْنَاهُمَا: غَلَبَ عَلَيْهِ وَقَهَرَهُ.
text.en: The bābs of the six-letter verb are all intransitive except the bāb of istafʿala, which is shared between the intransitive and the transitive, and two words of the bāb of ifʿanlā, which are transitive: israndāhu and ighrandāhu; their meaning is: he overcame him and subdued him.

lessons.title: The meanings of afʿala and istafʿala
body: “The hamza of afʿala comes for several meanings.” Making transitive: akramtuhu, “I honoured him”. Becoming (ṣayrūra): amshā al-rajulu, “the man came to own livestock (māshiya)”. Finding (wijdān): abkhaltuhu, “I found him miserly”. The time arriving (ḥaynūna): aḥṣada al-zarʿu, “the crop was ready for harvest”. Removing (izāla): ashkaytuhu, “I removed his complaint”. Entering (dukhūl): aṣbaḥa al-rajulu, “the man entered the morning”. Abundance (kathra): albana al-rajulu, “the man had much milk”.

“The sīn of istafʿala comes for several meanings.” Seeking (ṭalab): astaghfiru llāha, “I seek God's forgiveness”. Asking (suʾāl): istakhbara, “he asked for news”. Turning into (taḥawwul): istakhalla al-khamru, “the wine turned into vinegar (khall)”. Holding to be (iʿtiqād): istakramtuhu, “I held him noble”. Finding (wijdān): istajadtu shayʾan, “I found something good”. Saying the formula (taslīm): istarjaʿa al-qawmu ʿinda al-muṣībati, “the people said, at the calamity, innā li-llāhi wa-innā ilayhi rājiʿūn”, “we belong to God and to Him we return”.

These lists are the beginning of the study of meaning in ṣarf. They teach the student to ask, of every augmented verb, what its added letter has done to the root: made it transitive, made it a state, made it a judgement, made it a request. A dictionary gives the meaning of a word; the patterns explain it.

Notice that some meanings recur across patterns: “finding” is in both lists (abkhaltuhu, istajadtu), and “seeking” is in istafʿala as the Binā already said. The madrasa memorises the lists with their examples, as here.

text.original: وَهَمْزَةُ أَفْعَلَ يَجِيءُ لِمَعَانٍ: لِلتَّعْدِيَةِ نَحْوُ أَكْرَمْتُهُ، وَلِلصَّيْرُورَةِ نَحْوُ أَمْشَى الرَّجُلُ أَيْ صَارَ ذَا مَاشِيَةٍ، وَلِلْوِجْدَانِ نَحْوُ أَبْخَلْتُهُ أَيْ وَجَدْتُهُ بَخِيلًا، وَلِلْحَيْنُونَةِ نَحْوُ أَحْصَدَ الزَّرْعُ أَيْ حَانَ وَقْتُ حَصَادِهِ، وَلِلْإِزَالَةِ نَحْوُ أَشْكَيْتُهُ أَيْ أَزَلْتُ عَنْهُ الشِّكَايَةَ، وَلِلدُّخُولِ فِي الشَّيْءِ نَحْوُ أَصْبَحَ الرَّجُلُ إِذَا دَخَلَ فِي الصَّبَاحِ، وَلِلْكَثْرَةِ نَحْوُ أَلْبَنَ الرَّجُلُ إِذَا كَثُرَ عِنْدَهُ اللَّبَنُ.
text.en: The hamza of afʿala comes for several meanings: for transitivity, as akramtuhu “I honoured him”; for becoming, as amshā al-rajulu, that is, the man came to own cattle; for finding, as abkhaltuhu, that is, I found him miserly; for the time having come, as aḥṣada al-zarʿu, that is, the time of its harvest has come; for removal, as ashkaytuhu, that is, I removed his complaint; for entering into a thing, as aṣbaḥa al-rajulu, when he enters upon the morning; and for abundance, as albana al-rajulu, when he has much milk.

text.original: وَسِينُ اسْتَفْعَلَ يَجِيءُ لِمَعَانٍ: لِلطَّلَبِ نَحْوُ أَسْتَغْفِرُ اللَّهَ أَيْ أَطْلُبُ الْمَغْفِرَةَ، وَلِلسُّؤَالِ نَحْوُ اسْتَخْبَرَ أَيْ سَأَلَ الْخَبَرَ، وَلِلتَّحَوُّلِ نَحْوُ اسْتَخَلَّ الْخَمْرُ أَيِ انْقَلَبَ الْخَمْرُ خَلًّا، وَلِلِاعْتِقَادِ نَحْوُ اسْتَكْرَمْتُهُ أَيِ اعْتَقَدْتُ أَنَّهُ كَرِيمٌ، وَلِلْوِجْدَانِ نَحْوُ اسْتَجَدْتُ شَيْئًا أَيْ وَجَدْتُهُ جَيِّدًا، وَلِلتَّسْلِيمِ نَحْوُ قَوْلِهِمْ: اسْتَرْجَعَ الْقَوْمُ عِنْدَ الْمُصِيبَةِ، أَيْ قَالُوا: إِنَّا لِلَّهِ وَإِنَّا إِلَيْهِ رَاجِعُونَ.
text.en: The sīn of istafʿala comes for several meanings: for asking, as astaghfiru Allāha, that is, I ask for forgiveness; for enquiring, as istakhbara, that is, he asked for the news; for changing, as istakhalla al-khamru, that is, the wine turned into vinegar; for holding a belief, as istakramtuhu, that is, I held that he was noble; for finding, as istajadtu shayʾan, that is, I found it good; and for submission, as their saying istarjaʿa al-qawmu ʿinda al-muṣībati, that is, they said innā li-Allāhi wa-innā ilayhi rājiʿūna “we belong to God, and to Him we return”.

lessons.title: The weak letters and the classes
body: “The letters of length (madd), of softness (līn), of increase and of weakness (ʿilla) are one: the wāw, the yāʾ and the alif.” Four names for three letters, each name for one of their sides: they lengthen a vowel, they are soft to say, they are the commonest added letters, and they change and drop.

A past verb with one of them first is called weak and mithāl, “resembling”, “because it resembles the sound verb in bearing the vowels”: waʿada, yasara. With one in the middle, ajwaf, “hollow”: qāla, bāʿa. At the end, nāqiṣ, “defective”: ghazā, ramā. With two, joined lafīf if they are the ʿayn and the lām (rawiya, shawā), separated lafīf if they are the fāʾ and the lām (waqā).

“Every verb whose ʿayn and lām are of one kind, the first assimilated into the second because of heaviness, is called doubled”: madda. And every verb with a hamza is mahmūz al-fāʾ, al-ʿayn or al-lām by its place: akhadha, saʾala, qaraʾa. “Every verb free of these six classes is called sound (ṣaḥīḥ)”, and its conjugation has been given; “we shall now give the treatment of the six classes briefly.”

The Maqṣūd's classes are those of the Binā, and its last chapter is the reason for this lesson: from here on each change of a weak letter is explained from its base. The conjugation tool, which gives sound roots only, stops here; every form in the next eleven lessons comes from the print.

terms.en: the letters of length and softness: w, y, ā
weak in the fāʾ; it resembles the sound verb
hollow: weak in the ʿayn
defective: weak in the lām
two weak letters, joined or separated

examples.en: waʿada, yasara: mithāl
qāla, bāʿa: ajwaf
ghazā, ramā: nāqiṣ
rawiya, shawā: joined lafīf; waqā: separated lafīf

tasks.prompt: Give the four names of the wāw, yāʾ and alif and what each name says about them.
tasks.answer: Letters of length (madd): they lengthen a vowel. Of softness (līn): they are soft to say. Of increase (zawāʾid): they are among the commonest added letters. Of weakness (ʿilla): they change and drop.

tasks.prompt: Why is the verb weak in its fāʾ called mithāl?
tasks.answer: Because it resembles (yumāthilu) the sound verb in bearing the vowels: in its past, waʿada, the wāw takes a vowel like any sound letter.

tasks.prompt: Name the class: bāʿa; rawiya; saʾala; waqā; madda; kataba.
tasks.arabic: بَاعَ — رَوِيَ — سَأَلَ — وَقَى — مَدَّ — كَتَبَ
tasks.answer: Bāʿa: ajwaf. Rawiya: joined lafīf. Saʾala: mahmūz al-ʿayn. Waqā: separated lafīf. Madda: doubled. Kataba: sound.

quiz.prompt: Which letters are the letters of weakness?
quiz.explanation: Also called the letters of length, softness and increase.

quiz.prompt: Why is the mithāl so named?
options: It resembles the sound verb in bearing the vowels
quiz.explanation: Waʿada takes its vowels like naṣara.

quiz.prompt: Bāʿa is…
quiz.explanation: Weak in the ʿayn (b-y-ʿ).

quiz.prompt: Shawā is…
quiz.explanation: Weak ʿayn and lām side by side.

quiz.prompt: Why is the doubled verb assimilated?
quiz.explanation: “Because of heaviness” (li-thiqal).

quiz.prompt: What is a sound (ṣaḥīḥ) verb in the Maqṣūd?
options: One free of the six classes
quiz.explanation: No weak letter, doubling or hamza.

quiz.prompt: Where do the forms of the weak verbs in the next lessons come from?
quiz.explanation: The tool gives sound roots only.

text.original: وَحُرُوفُ الْمَدِّ وَاللِّينِ وَالزَّوَائِدِ وَالْعِلَّةِ وَاحِدَةٌ، وَهِيَ الْوَاوُ وَالْيَاءُ وَالْأَلِفُ. وَكُلُّ فِعْلٍ مَاضٍ فِي أَوَّلِهِ حَرْفٌ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْحُرُوفِ يُسَمَّى مُعْتَلًّا وَمِثَالًا لِمُمَاثَلَتِهِ الصَّحِيحَ فِي احْتِمَالِ الْحَرَكَاتِ، نَحْوُ: وَعَدَ وَيَسَرَ، وَإِنْ كَانَ فِي وَسَطِهِ يُسَمَّى أَجْوَفَ، نَحْوُ: قَالَ وَبَاعَ، وَإِنْ كَانَ فِي آخِرِهِ يُسَمَّى نَاقِصًا، نَحْوُ: غَزَا وَرَمَى.
text.en: The letters of prolongation and softness, the added letters and the letters of weakness are one: they are wāw, yāʾ and alif. Every past verb that has one of these letters at its beginning is called weak (muʿtall) and mithāl, because it is like (mumāthil) the sound verb in bearing the vowels, as waʿada “to promise” and yasara “to be easy”; if it is in its middle, it is called ajwaf, as qāla “to say” and bāʿa “to sell”; and if it is at its end, it is called nāqiṣ, as ghazā “to raid” and ramā “to throw”.

text.original: وَإِنْ كَانَ فِيهِ حَرْفَانِ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْحُرُوفِ، فَإِنْ كَانَا عَيْنَهُ وَلَامَهُ يُسَمَّى لَفِيفًا مَقْرُونًا، نَحْوُ: رَوِيَ وَشَوَى، وَإِنْ كَانَا فَاءَهُ وَلَامَهُ يُسَمَّى لَفِيفًا مَفْرُوقًا، نَحْوُ: وَقَى. وَكُلُّ فِعْلٍ عَيْنُهُ وَلَامُهُ حَرْفَانِ مِنْ جِنْسٍ وَاحِدٍ يُدْغَمُ أَوَّلُهُمَا فِي الْآخَرِ لِثِقَلٍ يُسَمَّى مُضَاعَفًا، نَحْوُ: مَدَّ.
text.en: If it has two of these letters: if they are its ʿayn and its lām, it is called joined lafīf, as rawiya “to quench one's thirst” and shawā “to roast”; if they are its fāʾ and its lām, it is called separated lafīf, as waqā “to guard”. Every verb whose ʿayn and lām are two letters of one kind, the first of which is assimilated into the other because of heaviness, is called muḍāʿaf, as madda “to stretch”.

text.original: وَكُلُّ فِعْلٍ فِيهِ هَمْزَةٌ، فَإِنْ كَانَتْ فِي أَوَّلِهِ يُسَمَّى مَهْمُوزَ الْفَاءِ، نَحْوُ: أَخَذَ، وَإِنْ كَانَتْ فِي وَسَطِهِ يُسَمَّى مَهْمُوزَ الْعَيْنِ، نَحْوُ: سَأَلَ، وَإِنْ كَانَتْ فِي آخِرِهِ يُسَمَّى مَهْمُوزَ اللَّامِ، نَحْوُ: قَرَأَ. وَكُلُّ فِعْلٍ خَالٍ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْأَقْسَامِ السِّتَّةِ يُسَمَّى صَحِيحًا، وَقُدِّمَ بَحْثُهُ فِي بَابِ الصَّحِيحِ، وَسَنَذْكُرُ بَحْثَ الْأَقْسَامِ السِّتَّةِ عَلَى سَبِيلِ الِاخْتِصَارِ.
text.en: Every verb in which there is a hamza: if it is at its beginning, it is called mahmūz al-fāʾ, as akhadha “to take”; if it is in its middle, it is called mahmūz al-ʿayn, as saʾala “to ask”; and if it is at its end, it is called mahmūz al-lām, as qaraʾa “to read”. Every verb free of these six divisions is called sound (ṣaḥīḥ); its discussion came first in the chapter on the sound verb, and we shall mention the discussion of the six divisions by way of brevity.

parts.title: The weak, doubled and hamzated verbs

lessons.title: Wāw and yāʾ become alif
body: The first rule of the weak verbs: “the wāw and the yāʾ, when they have a vowel and the letter before them has a fatḥa, turn into an alif”. So qāla and kāla, from roots with wāw and yāʾ in the middle; and in the defective verb, ghazā and ramā, from roots ending in wāw and yāʾ. The alif one sees is not a root letter but a wāw or a yāʾ in disguise.

Where the rule does not apply, the letter shows. In the dual: ghazawā, ramayā, the wāw and yāʾ keep their place. In the women's plural, the forms of the person addressed and of the speaker, the wāw and yāʾ have a sukūn of their own, and “a quiescent wāw or yāʾ turns into an alif only where its sukūn is not original”, where its vowel has moved to the letter before it, as in aqāma and abāʿa.

The plural of the men: ghazaw and ramaw. Their base is ghazawū and ramayū. By the rule the wāw and yāʾ turn into alif; two quiescent letters then meet, the alif and the wāw of the plural; and the alif drops. What is left is ghazaw, ramaw, with a fatḥa before the wāw of the plural that tells where the lost letter was.

The dual of the women: ghazatā and ramatā, from ghazawatā and ramayatā. The wāw and yāʾ turn into alif; the alif drops because it meets the tāʾ, whose sukūn is original (as in ghazat, ramat); the tāʾ took a vowel only because of the alif of the dual, “and its vowel is accidental, and the accidental is as if it did not exist”. This last saying is a key to many changes in ṣarf.

terms.en: turning one letter into another
an original sukūn
the accidental is as if it did not exist
the meeting of two quiescent letters

examples.en: qāla, kāla, ghazā, ramā: a vowelled wāw or yāʾ after a fatḥa becomes alif
ghazawā, ramayā: the dual, no change
ghazaw, ramaw, from ghazawū and ramayū
ghazatā, ramatā, from ghazawatā and ramayatā

tasks.prompt: Explain, as the Maqṣūd does, how ramayū becomes ramaw.
tasks.answer: The yāʾ has a vowel and a fatḥa before it, so it turns into an alif; the alif meets the quiescent wāw of the plural; two quiescent letters cannot meet, so the alif drops: ramaw.

tasks.prompt: Why do ghazawā and ramayā keep their wāw and yāʾ?
tasks.answer: The book only states that they are not turned into alif in the dual. The usual reason: turned into alif, the root's alif would meet the alif of the dual, one would drop, and the dual would look like the singular, ghazā.

tasks.prompt: Why does the alif drop in ghazatā, though the tāʾ there has a vowel?
tasks.answer: The tāʾ's sukūn is original (ghazat); it took a fatḥa only because of the alif of the dual. That vowel is accidental, and the accidental counts as if it did not exist, so the alif drops as before a quiescent letter.

quiz.prompt: When do the wāw and yāʾ turn into alif?
options: When they have a vowel and a fatḥa comes before them
At the start of a word
quiz.explanation: Qāla, kāla, ghazā, ramā.

quiz.prompt: What is the base of ghazaw?
quiz.explanation: The wāw became alif, then the alif dropped.

quiz.prompt: Ramayā is…
quiz.explanation: No change in the dual.

quiz.prompt: What does “the accidental is as if it did not exist” explain here?
options: Why the alif drops in ghazatā
quiz.explanation: The tāʾ's vowel came only for the dual.

quiz.prompt: Ghazatā means…
quiz.explanation: Ghazatā is the dual of the absent women, from ghazawatā, with the wāw turned to alif and dropped.

quiz.prompt: In which form does a quiescent wāw turn into alif?
options: Where its vowel has moved to the letter before, as in aqāma
quiz.explanation: Its sukūn must not be original.

quiz.prompt: The alif of qāla is…
quiz.explanation: The root of qāla is q-w-l: its alif is a vowelled wāw after a fatḥa, turned into alif.

text.original: الْوَاوُ وَالْيَاءُ إِذَا تَحَرَّكَتَا وَانْفَتَحَ مَا قَبْلَهُمَا قُلِبَتَا أَلِفًا، نَحْوُ: قَالَ وَكَالَ، مِثَالُهُمَا مِنَ النَّاقِصِ: غَزَا وَرَمَى، وَتَقُولُ فِي تَثْنِيَتِهِمَا: غَزَوَا وَرَمَيَا، فَلَا تُقْلَبَانِ أَلِفًا، وَلَا تُقْلَبَانِ أَيْضًا فِي جَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ وَالْمُوَاجَهَةِ وَنَفْسِ الْمُتَكَلِّمِ؛ لِأَنَّ الْوَاوَ السَّاكِنَةَ وَالْيَاءَ السَّاكِنَةَ لَا تُقْلَبَانِ أَلِفًا إِلَّا فِي مَوْضِعٍ يَكُونُ سُكُونُهُمَا غَيْرَ أَصْلِيٍّ، بِأَنْ نُقِلَتْ حَرَكَتُهُمَا إِلَى مَا قَبْلَهُمَا، نَحْوُ: أَقَامَ وَأَبَاعَ.
text.en: Wāw and yāʾ, when they are vowelled and the letter before them has a fatḥa, are turned into alif, as qāla and kāla; their example from the defective is ghazā and ramā. You say in their dual ghazawā and ramayā, and they are not turned into alif; nor are they turned in the feminine plural, the forms of address and the speaker himself; for wāw and yāʾ with sukūn are turned into alif only where their sukūn is not original, in that their vowel has been moved to the letter before them, as aqāma “to set up” and abāʿa “to offer for sale”.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي الْجَمْعِ: غَزَوْا وَرَمَوْا، وَالْأَصْلُ غَزَوُوا وَرَمَيُوا، قُلِبَتَا أَلِفًا لِتَحَرُّكِهِمَا وَانْفِتَاحِ مَا قَبْلَهُمَا، فَاجْتَمَعَ سَاكِنَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الْأَلِفُ الْمَقْلُوبَةُ، وَالثَّانِي وَاوُ الْجَمْعِ، فَحُذِفَ الْأَلِفُ الْمَقْلُوبَةُ، فَبَقِيَ غَزَوْا وَرَمَوْا.
text.en: You say in the plural ghazaw and ramaw; the origin is ghazawū and ramayū: they were turned into alif because they were vowelled and the letter before them had a fatḥa, so two unvowelled letters met: one the alif that had been turned, the other the wāw of the plural; so the turned alif was dropped, and ghazaw and ramaw remained.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي تَثْنِيَةِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ: غَزَتَا وَرَمَتَا، وَالْأَصْلُ غَزَوَتَا وَرَمَيَتَا، قُلِبَتَا أَلِفًا لِتَحَرُّكِهِمَا وَانْفِتَاحِ مَا قَبْلَهُمَا، وَحُذِفَتِ الْأَلِفُ لِسُكُونِهَا وَسُكُونِ التَّاءِ؛ لِأَنَّ التَّاءَ كَانَتْ سَاكِنَةً فِي الْأَصْلِ، فَحُرِّكَتِ التَّاءُ لِأَلِفِ التَّثْنِيَةِ، فَحَرَكَتُهَا عَارِضَةٌ، وَالْعَارِضُ كَالْمَعْدُومِ.
text.en: You say in the feminine dual ghazatā and ramatā; the origin is ghazawatā and ramayatā: they were turned into alif because they were vowelled and the letter before them had a fatḥa, and the alif was dropped because it and the tāʾ were unvowelled, for the tāʾ was unvowelled in origin; the tāʾ was given a vowel for the alif of the dual, so its vowel is accidental, and the accidental is as though it did not exist.

lessons.title: Qulna and kilna; the yāʾ after kasra and ḍamma
body: The women's plural of the hollow verb: qulna and kilna, “they (women) said, measured”. Their base is qawalna and kayalna. The wāw and yāʾ turn into alif (vowelled, after a fatḥa); the alif drops because it meets the quiescent lām; this leaves qalna and kalna, with a fatḥa on the first letter.

“Then the fatḥa of the qāf was moved to a ḍamma, and that of the kāf to a kasra, so that the ḍamma would point to the dropped wāw and the kasra to the dropped yāʾ; for what is born of the ḍamma is the wāw, of the kasra the yāʾ, and of the fatḥa the alif.” The vowel left behind is a sign of the letter that has gone: qulna tells you the root has a wāw, kilna that it has a yāʾ. The same holds in qultu, “I said”, and kiltu.

Two more rules. A yāʾ after a kasra stays as it is, quiescent, or with a vowel if that vowel is a fatḥa: khashiya, “he feared”, khashītu, “I feared”. And a quiescent yāʾ after a ḍamma turns into a wāw: aysara yūsiru, “to be well off”, whose base is yuysiru.

Behind all these lies one idea that the book has just stated: each short vowel has its long letter, ḍamma with wāw, kasra with yāʾ, fatḥa with alif. A weak letter tends to follow the vowel before it; and when it drops, the vowel stays to remember it.

terms.en: what is born of the ḍamma: the wāw
hollow with wāw, hollow with yāʾ
pointing to the dropped letter

examples.en: qulna, kilna: from qawalna and kayalna
qalna, kalna: the step before, with the alif dropped
khashiya, khashītu: a yāʾ after kasra stays
aysara yūsiru: a quiescent yāʾ after ḍamma becomes wāw

tasks.prompt: Explain step by step how qawalna becomes qulna.
tasks.answer: The wāw has a vowel and a fatḥa before it, so it turns into an alif; the alif meets the quiescent lām and drops, leaving qalna; then the fatḥa of the qāf becomes a ḍamma to point to the dropped wāw: qulna.

tasks.prompt: Why kilna with a kasra and not kulna?
tasks.answer: Because the dropped letter of k-y-l is a yāʾ, and the vowel born of the yāʾ is the kasra; the ḍamma would point to a wāw.

tasks.prompt: What is the base of yūsiru, and which rule changes it?
tasks.answer: Yuysiru. A quiescent yāʾ after a ḍamma turns into a wāw: yūsiru.

quiz.prompt: What is the base of qulna?
quiz.explanation: Qulna is faʿalna on q-w-l: qawalna, before the wāw turned into alif and dropped.

quiz.prompt: Why does qulna have a ḍamma on the qāf?
options: To point to the dropped wāw
quiz.explanation: What is born of the ḍamma is the wāw.

quiz.prompt: Which vowel is born of the yāʾ, as the book puts it?
quiz.explanation: The book says the yāʾ is born of the kasra, the wāw of the ḍamma, the alif of the fatḥa: hence kilna.

quiz.prompt: In khashītu, the yāʾ…
quiz.explanation: A yāʾ after kasra stays.

quiz.prompt: What is the base of yūsiru?
quiz.explanation: Quiescent yāʾ after ḍamma → wāw.

quiz.prompt: What is left after the alif drops from qālna?
quiz.explanation: Then the vowel is changed: qulna.

quiz.prompt: Kilna means…
quiz.explanation: From kāla, root k-y-l.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي جَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ مِنَ الْأَجْوَفِ: قُلْنَ وَكِلْنَ، وَالْأَصْلُ قَوَلْنَ وَكَيَلْنَ، قُلِبَتَا أَلِفًا لِتَحَرُّكِهِمَا وَانْفِتَاحِ مَا قَبْلَهُمَا، ثُمَّ حُذِفَتِ الْأَلِفُ لِسُكُونِهَا وَسُكُونِ اللَّامِ، فَبَقِيَ قَلْنَ وَكَلْنَ بِفَتْحِ الْقَافِ وَالْكَافِ،
text.en: You say in the feminine plural of the hollow qulna and kilna; the origin is qawalna and kayalna: they were turned into alif because they were vowelled and the letter before them had a fatḥa; then the alif was dropped because it and the lām were unvowelled, and qalna and kalna remained, with fatḥa on the qāf and the kāf;

text.original: ثُمَّ نُقِلَتْ فَتْحَةُ الْقَافِ إِلَى الضَّمَّةِ وَالْكَافِ إِلَى الْكَسْرَةِ، لِتَدُلَّ الضَّمَّةُ عَلَى الْوَاوِ الْمَحْذُوفَةِ وَالْكَسْرَةُ عَلَى الْيَاءِ الْمَحْذُوفَةِ؛ لِأَنَّ الْمُتَوَلِّدَ مِنَ الضَّمَّةِ الْوَاوُ، وَمِنَ الْكَسْرَةِ الْيَاءُ، وَمِنَ الْفَتْحَةِ الْأَلِفُ.
text.en: then the fatḥa of the qāf was changed to a ḍamma, and that of the kāf to a kasra, so that the ḍamma should point to the dropped wāw and the kasra to the dropped yāʾ; for what is born of the ḍamma is the wāw, of the kasra the yāʾ, and of the fatḥa the alif.

text.original: وَالْيَاءُ إِذَا انْكَسَرَ مَا قَبْلَهَا تُرِكَتْ عَلَى حَالِهَا سَاكِنَةً، أَوْ مُتَحَرِّكَةً إِذَا كَانَتِ الْحَرَكَةُ فَتْحَةً، نَحْوُ: خَشِيَ وَخَشِيتُ. وَالْيَاءُ السَّاكِنَةُ إِذَا انْضَمَّ مَا قَبْلَهَا قُلِبَتْ وَاوًا، نَحْوُ: أَيْسَرَ يُوسِرُ، أَصْلُهُ يُيْسِرُ.
text.en: The yāʾ, when the letter before it has a kasra, is left as it is, unvowelled, or vowelled if the vowel is a fatḥa, as khashiya “he feared” and khashītu “I feared”. The unvowelled yāʾ, when the letter before it has a ḍamma, is turned into wāw, as aysara yūsiru “to become rich”; its origin is yuysiru.

lessons.title: The passive of the weak verbs: qīla, duʿiya, ghuzū
body: The passive of the hollow verb: qīla, “it was said”, from quwila. “The ḍamma of the qāf before the kasra of the wāw was felt heavy; the qāf was made quiescent and the kasra of the wāw moved to it; so the qāf took a kasra and the wāw a sukūn; then the wāw turned into a yāʾ, because a quiescent wāw after a kasra becomes a yāʾ.” Three steps: the vowel moves back, the wāw is left quiescent, and the wāw follows the kasra.

A vowelled wāw at the end of a word after a kasra becomes a yāʾ: ghabiya, “to be dull”, from ghabiwa, the root of al-ghabāwa, dullness, “the opposite of understanding”. And so duʿiya, the passive of daʿā, “to call”, from duʿiwa. The yāʾ you see in duʿiya is a wāw that followed the kasra.

The plural of the men of the passive defective: ghuzū, “they were raided”, from ghuziyū (the wāw had already become yāʾ in ghuziya). “The zāy was made quiescent, the ḍamma of the yāʾ moved to the zāy, and the yāʾ dropped because it met the quiescent wāw of the plural”: ghuzū.

Notice the method. Every form is explained from a base built on the regular pattern, fuʿila and fuʿilū, and one or two short rules lead from the base to the form. A student who knows the rules does not need a separate table for each weak verb; he needs the regular pattern and the rules.

moving a vowel to the letter before
the base form on the regular pattern

tasks.prompt: Explain step by step how quwila becomes qīla.
tasks.answer: The ḍamma of the qāf before the kasra of the wāw is heavy: the qāf loses its ḍamma and takes the kasra of the wāw; the wāw is now quiescent after a kasra, so it turns into a yāʾ: qīla.

tasks.prompt: Why is the passive of daʿā written duʿiya with a yāʾ, though the root ends in a wāw?
tasks.answer: Its base is duʿiwa: a vowelled wāw at the end of the word after a kasra turns into a yāʾ.

tasks.prompt: Give the base of ghuzū and the two changes that lead to it.
tasks.answer: Ghuziyū. The ḍamma of the yāʾ moves to the zāy (which loses its kasra), and the yāʾ, now quiescent, drops before the quiescent wāw of the plural: ghuzū.

quiz.prompt: What is the base of qīla?
quiz.explanation: Root q-w-l, passive fuʿila.

quiz.prompt: A quiescent wāw after a kasra…
quiz.explanation: Hence the yāʾ of qīla.

quiz.prompt: What is the base of ghabiya?
quiz.explanation: From al-ghabāwa, “dullness”.

quiz.prompt: Duʿiya is the passive of…
quiz.explanation: Duʿiya is fuʿila on d-ʿ-w: duʿiwa, whose final wāw after a kasra became a yāʾ.

quiz.prompt: Ghuzū means…
quiz.explanation: The passive plural of ghazā.

quiz.prompt: In quwila, which sequence was felt heavy?
options: A ḍamma before the kasra of the wāw
quiz.explanation: So the kasra moved back to the qāf.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي مَجْهُولِ الْأَجْوَفِ: قِيلَ، وَالْأَصْلُ قُوِلَ، فَاسْتُثْقِلَتْ ضَمَّةُ الْقَافِ قَبْلَ كَسْرَةِ الْوَاوِ، فَأُسْكِنَتِ الْقَافُ وَنُقِلَتْ كَسْرَةُ الْوَاوِ إِلَيْهَا، فَصَارَتِ الْقَافُ مَكْسُورَةً وَالْوَاوُ سَاكِنَةً، ثُمَّ قُلِبَتِ الْوَاوُ يَاءً؛ لِأَنَّ الْوَاوَ السَّاكِنَةَ إِذَا انْكَسَرَ مَا قَبْلَهَا قُلِبَتْ يَاءً.
text.en: You say in the passive of the hollow qīla “it was said”; the origin is quwila: the ḍamma of the qāf before the kasra of the wāw was felt heavy, so the qāf was made unvowelled and the kasra of the wāw was moved to it; the qāf then had a kasra and the wāw a sukūn; then the wāw was turned into yāʾ, for an unvowelled wāw is turned into yāʾ when the letter before it has a kasra.

text.original: وَالْوَاوُ الْمُتَحَرِّكَةُ إِذَا وَقَعَتْ فِي آخِرِ الْكَلِمَةِ وَانْكَسَرَ مَا قَبْلَهَا قُلِبَتْ يَاءً، نَحْوُ: غَبِيَ، وَالْأَصْلُ غَبِوَ مِنَ الْغَبَاوَةِ، وَالْغَبَاوَةُ عَكْسُ الْإِدْرَاكِ، وَكَذَا دُعِيَ مَجْهُولُ دَعَا، وَالْأَصْلُ دُعِوَ.
text.en: A vowelled wāw at the end of the word, when the letter before it has a kasra, is turned into yāʾ, as ghabiya “to be dull”; the origin is ghabiwa, from al-ghabāwati “dullness”, and dullness is the opposite of understanding; and so duʿiya, the passive of daʿā “to call”; the origin is duʿiwa.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي جَمْعِ الْمُذَكَّرِ مِنْ مَجْهُولِ النَّاقِصِ: غُزُوا، وَالْأَصْلُ غُزِيُوا، فَأُسْكِنَتِ الزَّايُ، ثُمَّ نُقِلَتْ ضَمَّةُ الْيَاءِ إِلَى الزَّايِ، وَحُذِفَتِ الْيَاءُ لِسُكُونِهَا وَسُكُونِ الْوَاوِ، فَبَقِيَ غُزُوا.
text.en: You say in the masculine plural of the passive of the defective ghuzū; the origin is ghuziyū: the zāy was made unvowelled, then the ḍamma of the yāʾ was moved to the zāy, and the yāʾ was dropped because it and the wāw were unvowelled, and ghuzū remained.

lessons.title: The present of the hollow and the defective
body: The hollow present: “every wāw and yāʾ with a vowel, before which stands a quiescent sound letter, gives its vowel to the sound letter”. Yaqūlu from yaqwulu, yakīlu from yakyilu, yakhāfu from yakhwafu. The wāw and yāʾ, now quiescent after their own vowel, become long vowels; in yakhāfu the wāw became an alif, “because its sukūn is not original and a fatḥa comes before it”.

The defective present: a final wāw or yāʾ with a vowel, after a vowelled letter, is made quiescent unless it is in naṣb: yaghzū, yarmī, yakhshā, from yaghzuwu, yarmiyu, yakhshayu, “because the ḍamma is felt heavy on the wāw and the yāʾ”; and the yāʾ of yakhshā became an alif, being vowelled after a fatḥa. In naṣb they keep their vowel, “because the fatḥa is light on them”: lan yaghzuwa, lan yarmiya; but lan yakhshā, for an alif takes no vowel. The duals: yaghzuwāni, yarmiyāni, yakhshayāni.

The plural of the men: yaghzūna, yarmūna, yakhshawna, from yaghzuwūna, yarmiyūna, yakhshayūna. The wāw and yāʾ were made quiescent (the ḍamma being heavy on them); two quiescent letters met, the weak letter and the wāw of the plural, and the first dropped. In yakhshayūna the yāʾ first turned into alif and then dropped, leaving the fatḥa: yakhshawna; and in yarmūna the mīm took a ḍamma “so that the wāw of the plural would be sound”.

The woman addressed: taghzīna, from taghzuwīna. The zāy was made quiescent, its ḍamma being heavy before the kasra of the wāw, and took that kasra; the wāw dropped before the quiescent yāʾ of the woman addressed. Each step is one of the rules already met: a heavy vowel removed, a vowel moved back, a letter dropped where two quiescent letters meet.

terms.en: giving the vowel to the quiescent letter before
making the weak letter quiescent
the lightness of the fatḥa, said on wāw and yāʾ

examples.en: yaqūlu, yakīlu, yakhāfu: from yaqwulu, yakyilu, yakhwafu
yaghzū, yarmī, yakhshā: the final weak letter made quiescent

tasks.prompt: Explain how yakhwafu becomes yakhāfu.
tasks.answer: The vowelled wāw stands after a quiescent sound letter (the khāʾ), so it gives its fatḥa to the khāʾ; the wāw is now quiescent with a fatḥa before it, and its sukūn is not original, so it turns into an alif: yakhāfu.

tasks.prompt: Why do we say lan yarmiya with a fatḥa on the yāʾ, but yarmī without a ḍamma?
tasks.answer: The ḍamma is felt heavy on the yāʾ, so in rafʿ the yāʾ is made quiescent (yarmī); the fatḥa is light, so in naṣb it is said (lan yarmiya).

tasks.prompt: Explain the fatḥa before the wāw in yakhshawna and the ḍamma in yarmūna.
tasks.answer: Yakhshayūna: the yāʾ turned into alif (vowelled after a fatḥa) and dropped before the wāw of the plural, leaving the fatḥa: yakhshawna. Yarmiyūna: the yāʾ was made quiescent and dropped, and the mīm took a ḍamma so that the wāw of the plural would be sound: yarmūna.

tasks.prompt: Give the base of taghzīna and its changes.
tasks.answer: Taghzuwīna. The ḍamma of the zāy before the kasra of the wāw is heavy: the zāy takes the kasra of the wāw; the wāw, now quiescent, drops before the quiescent yāʾ: taghzīna.

quiz.prompt: What is the base of yaqūlu?
quiz.explanation: The wāw gave its ḍamma to the qāf.

quiz.prompt: Why is the wāw of yakhāfu an alif?
options: Its sukūn is not original and a fatḥa comes before it
quiz.explanation: The wāw of yakhwafu gave its fatḥa to the khāʾ; a quiescent wāw whose sukūn is not original, after a fatḥa, becomes alif.

quiz.prompt: Which vowel is said on the final wāw and yāʾ of the present?
quiz.explanation: Lan yaghzuwa, lan yarmiya.

quiz.prompt: Why is lan yakhshā without a fatḥa?
quiz.explanation: The naṣb is assumed on the alif.

quiz.prompt: What is the base of yarmūna?
quiz.explanation: The yāʾ dropped and the mīm took a ḍamma.

quiz.prompt: Yakhshayāni is…
quiz.explanation: In the dual the weak letter shows.

quiz.prompt: Taghzīna is the form of…
quiz.explanation: Taghzīna is said to a woman, from taghzuwīna: the wāw dropped before the yāʾ of the woman addressed.

text.original: وَكُلُّ وَاوٍ وَيَاءٍ مُتَحَرِّكَتَيْنِ يَكُونُ مَا قَبْلَهُمَا حَرْفًا صَحِيحًا سَاكِنًا نُقِلَتْ حَرَكَتُهُمَا إِلَى الْحَرْفِ الصَّحِيحِ، نَحْوُ: يَقُولُ وَيَكِيلُ وَيَخَافُ، وَالْأَصْلُ يَقْوُلُ وَيَكْيِلُ وَيَخْوَفُ، وَإِنَّمَا قُلِبَتْ وَاوُ يَخَافُ أَلِفًا لِكَوْنِ سُكُونِهَا غَيْرَ أَصْلِيٍّ وَانْفِتَاحِ مَا قَبْلَهَا.
text.en: Every vowelled wāw and yāʾ before which there is an unvowelled sound letter: their vowel is moved to the sound letter, as yaqūlu “he says”, yakīlu “he measures” and yakhāfu “he fears”; the origin is yaqwulu, yakyilu and yakhwafu; the wāw of yakhāfu was turned into alif only because its sukūn is not original and the letter before it has a fatḥa.

text.original: وَكُلُّ وَاوٍ وَيَاءٍ إِذَا كَانَتَا مُتَحَرِّكَتَيْنِ وَوَقَعَتَا فِي لَامِ الْفِعْلِ وَمَا قَبْلَهُمَا حَرْفٌ مُتَحَرِّكٌ أُسْكِنَتَا مَا لَمْ يَكُنْ مَنْصُوبًا، نَحْوُ: يَغْزُو وَيَرْمِي وَيَخْشَى، لِاسْتِثْقَالِ الضَّمَّةِ عَلَى الْوَاوِ وَالْيَاءِ، وَالْأَصْلُ يَغْزُوُ وَيَرْمِيُ وَيَخْشَيُ، قُلِبَتْ يَاءُ يَخْشَى أَلِفًا لِتَحَرُّكِهَا وَانْفِتَاحِ مَا قَبْلَهَا.
text.en: Every wāw and yāʾ, when they are vowelled, fall in the lām of the verb and the letter before them is vowelled, are made unvowelled as long as they are not in naṣb, as yaghzū “he raids”, yarmī “he throws” and yakhshā “he fears”, because the ḍamma is felt heavy on wāw and yāʾ; the origin is yaghzuwu, yarmiyu and yakhshayu; the yāʾ of yakhshā was turned into alif because it was vowelled and the letter before it had a fatḥa.

text.original: وَتُحَرَّكُ الْوَاوُ وَالْيَاءُ إِذَا كَانَتَا مَنْصُوبَتَيْنِ، نَحْوُ: لَنْ يَغْزُوَ وَلَنْ يَرْمِيَ وَلَنْ يَخْشَى، لِخِفَّةِ الْفَتْحَةِ عَلَيْهِمَا. وَتَقُولُ فِي التَّثْنِيَةِ: يَغْزُوَانِ وَيَرْمِيَانِ وَيَخْشَيَانِ.
text.en: The wāw and the yāʾ are given a vowel when they are in naṣb, as lan yaghzuwa, wa-lan yarmiya and wa-lan yakhshā, because the fatḥa is light on them. You say in the dual yaghzuwāni, yarmiyāni and yakhshayāni.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي الْجَمْعِ: يَغْزُونَ وَيَرْمُونَ وَيَخْشَوْنَ، وَالْأَصْلُ يَغْزُوُونَ وَيَرْمِيُونَ وَيَخْشَيُونَ، فَأُسْكِنَتِ الْوَاوُ وَالْيَاءُ لِوُقُوعِهِمَا فِي لَامِ الْفِعْلِ وَاسْتِثْقَالِ الضَّمَّةِ عَلَيْهِمَا، فَاجْتَمَعَ سَاكِنَانِ: الْوَاوُ وَالْيَاءُ، وَبَعْدَهُمَا وَاوُ الْجَمْعِ، فَحُذِفَ مَا كَانَ قَبْلَ وَاوِ الْجَمْعِ،
text.en: You say in the plural yaghzūna, yarmūna and yakhshawna; the origin is yaghzuwūna, yarmiyūna and yakhshayūna: the wāw and the yāʾ were made unvowelled because they fall in the lām of the verb and the ḍamma is felt heavy on them, so two unvowelled letters met, the wāw or the yāʾ and after them the wāw of the plural; so what was before the wāw of the plural was dropped;

text.original: وَقُلِبَتْ يَاءُ يَخْشَيُونَ أَلِفًا لِتَحَرُّكِهَا وَانْفِتَاحِ مَا قَبْلَهَا، وَضُمَّتِ الْمِيمُ فِي يَرْمُونَ لِيَصِحَّ وَاوُ الْجَمْعِ. وَتَقُولُ فِي وَاحِدَةِ الْمُخَاطَبَةِ: تَغْزِينَ، وَالْأَصْلُ تَغْزُوِينَ، فَأُسْكِنَتِ الزَّايُ لِاسْتِثْقَالِ الضَّمَّةِ قَبْلَ كَسْرَةِ الْوَاوِ، وَنُقِلَتْ كَسْرَةُ الْوَاوِ إِلَى الزَّايِ، وَحُذِفَتِ الْوَاوُ لِسُكُونِهَا وَسُكُونِ الْيَاءِ.
text.en: and the yāʾ of yakhshayūna was turned into alif because it was vowelled and the letter before it had a fatḥa; and the mīm in yarmūna was given a ḍamma so that the wāw of the plural should be sound. You say in the singular feminine addressed taghzīna; the origin is taghzuwīna: the zāy was made unvowelled because the ḍamma before the kasra of the wāw was felt heavy, the kasra of the wāw was moved to the zāy, and the wāw was dropped because it and the yāʾ were unvowelled.

lessons.title: The participles of the weak verbs
body: The active participle of the hollow verb: qāʾil and kāʾil. In the past one has qāla and kāla; the alif of fāʿil is added, and “two alifs meet: the alif of the participle and the alif turned from the ʿayn of the verb; so the alif from the ʿayn was turned into a hamza”. That is why the participle of qāla has a hamza that its root does not have.

The active participle of the defective verb keeps its yāʾ in naṣb: raʾaytu ghāziyan wa-rāmiyan, “I saw a raider and a thrower”. In rafʿ and jarr: hādhā ghāzin wa-rāmin, marartu bi-ghāzin wa-rāmin, from ghāziyun and rāmiyun: the yāʾ was made quiescent, met the tanwīn, and dropped; the tanwīn stays. With the article the tanwīn goes and the yāʾ returns, quiescent: hādhā al-ghāzī wa-l-rāmī, marartu bi-l-ghāzī wa-l-rāmī.

The passive participle of the hollow verb: maqūl, from maqwūl, “treated as we said”: the vowel of the wāw moved back, and one of the two quiescent letters dropped. Of the verbs with yāʾ: makīl, from makyūl; the yāʾ's vowel moved to the kāf, the yāʾ dropped, and the kāf took a kasra to point to the yāʾ, “and when the kāf took a kasra, the wāw of the participle became a yāʾ”.

The passive participle of the defective verb: when two wāws meet, the first quiescent, they are assimilated: maghzuww, from maghzūw. When a wāw and a yāʾ meet, the first quiescent, the wāw turns into a yāʾ, the letter before takes a kasra, and the two yāʾs are assimilated: marmiyy and makhshiyy, from marmūy and makhshūy.

terms.en: turning the alif into a hamza: qāʾil
a noun ending in yāʾ after kasra: ghāzin, al-ghāzī
roots with a yāʾ
assimilation: maghzuww, marmiyy

raʾaytu ghāziyan wa-rāmiyan: the yāʾ kept in naṣb

examples.en: the yāʾ dropped before tanwīn; it returns with the article
maqūl from maqwūl; makīl from makyūl

tasks.prompt: Why does qāʾil have a hamza?
tasks.answer: The alif of fāʿil is added to qāla, whose middle is already an alif (from the wāw). Two alifs cannot stand together, so the alif from the root was turned into a hamza: qāʾil.

tasks.prompt: Give ghāzī in the three states without the article, and with it.
tasks.answer: Without the article: hādhā ghāzin (rafʿ), raʾaytu ghāziyan (naṣb), marartu bi-ghāzin (jarr). With the article: hādhā al-ghāzī, raʾaytu al-ghāziya, marartu bi-l-ghāzī.

tasks.prompt: Explain how makyūl becomes makīl.
tasks.answer: The yāʾ gives its vowel to the kāf; the yāʾ, now quiescent, drops before the quiescent wāw; the kāf takes a kasra to point to the dropped yāʾ; and the wāw after a kasra becomes a yāʾ: makīl.

tasks.prompt: Why is the passive participle of ramā marmiyy and not marmūy?
tasks.answer: In marmūy a quiescent wāw meets a yāʾ: the wāw turns into a yāʾ, the mīm before it takes a kasra, and the two yāʾs are assimilated: marmiyy.

quiz.prompt: Why is qāʾil written with a hamza?
options: Two alifs met and the root's alif became hamza
quiz.explanation: Alif of fāʿil + alif from the wāw.

quiz.prompt: Hādhā ghāzin: what happened to the yāʾ?
quiz.explanation: In ghāziyun the yāʾ was made quiescent, met the quiescent tanwīn, and dropped: ghāzin.

quiz.prompt: In raʾaytu ghāziyan, the yāʾ…
quiz.explanation: The fatḥa is light on the yāʾ.

quiz.prompt: With the article, ghāzin becomes…
quiz.explanation: The tanwīn goes and the yāʾ returns, quiescent.

quiz.prompt: The base of maqūl is…
quiz.explanation: Maqūl is mafʿūl on q-w-l: maqwūl, with one of the two quiescent letters dropped.

quiz.prompt: Maghzuww comes from…
quiz.explanation: The first wāw quiescent, the second vowelled.

quiz.prompt: What is the passive participle of khashiya?
quiz.explanation: Makhshūy: the wāw turned into yāʾ, the shīn took a kasra, and the two yāʾs were assimilated: makhshiyy.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي اسْمِ الْفَاعِلِ مِنَ الْأَجْوَفِ: قَائِلٌ وَكَائِلٌ، وَكَانَ فِي الْمَاضِي قَالَ وَكَالَ، فَزِيدَ الْأَلِفُ لِاسْمِ الْفَاعِلِ، فَاجْتَمَعَ أَلِفَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا أَلِفُ اسْمِ الْفَاعِلِ، وَالْآخَرُ الْأَلِفُ الْمَقْلُوبَةُ مِنْ عَيْنِ الْفِعْلِ، فَقُلِبَتِ الْأَلِفُ الْمَقْلُوبَةُ مِنْ عَيْنِ الْفِعْلِ هَمْزَةً، وَكَذَلِكَ كَائِلٌ.
text.en: You say in the active participle of the hollow qāʾilun “one who says” and kāʾilun “one who measures”. In the past it was qāla and kāla; the alif of the active participle was added, so two alifs met, one the alif of the active participle and the other the alif turned from the ʿayn of the verb; so the alif turned from the ʿayn of the verb was turned into hamza; and so also kāʾilun.

text.original: وَاسْمُ الْفَاعِلِ مِنَ النَّاقِصِ مَنْصُوبٌ فِي حَالَةِ النَّصْبِ، نَحْوُ: رَأَيْتُ غَازِيًا وَرَامِيًا، فَلَا يَتَغَيَّرُ صِيغَتُهُ. وَتَقُولُ فِي الرَّفْعِ وَالْجَرِّ: هَذَا غَازٍ وَرَامٍ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِغَازٍ وَرَامٍ، وَالْأَصْلُ غَازِيٌ وَرَامِيٌ، فَأُسْكِنَتِ الْيَاءُ كَمَا ذَكَرْنَا، فَاجْتَمَعَ سَاكِنَانِ: الْيَاءُ وَالتَّنْوِينُ، فَحُذِفَتِ الْيَاءُ وَبَقِيَ التَّنْوِينُ.
text.en: The active participle of the defective is in naṣb in the state of naṣb, as raʾaytu ghāziyan wa-rāmiyan “I saw a raider and a thrower”, and its form does not change. You say in rafʿ and jarr hādhā ghāzin wa-rāmin “this is a raider and a thrower” and marartu bi-ghāzin wa-rāmin “I passed by a raider and a thrower”; the origin is ghāziyun and rāmiyun: the yāʾ was made unvowelled as we have said, so two unvowelled letters met, the yāʾ and the tanwīn; so the yāʾ was dropped and the tanwīn remained.

text.original: فَإِنْ أَدْخَلْتَ الْأَلِفَ وَاللَّامَ سَقَطَ التَّنْوِينُ وَتَعُودُ الْيَاءُ سَاكِنَةً، فَتَقُولُ: هَذَا الْغَازِي وَالرَّامِي، وَمَرَرْتُ بِالْغَازِي وَالرَّامِي.
text.en: If you bring in the alif and lām, the tanwīn falls away and the yāʾ returns, unvowelled, and you say hādhā al-ghāzī wa-al-rāmī “this is the raider and the thrower” and marartu bi-al-ghāzī wa-al-rāmī “I passed by the raider and the thrower”.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي مَفْعُولِ الْأَجْوَفِ: مَقُولٌ، أَصْلُهُ مَقْوُولٌ، فَفُعِلَ بِهِ كَمَا ذَكَرْنَا. وَتَقُولُ فِي بَنَاتِ الْيَاءِ: مَكِيلٌ، وَالْأَصْلُ مَكْيُولٌ، فَنُقِلَتْ حَرَكَةُ الْيَاءِ إِلَى الْكَافِ، فَحُذِفَتِ الْيَاءُ لِاجْتِمَاعِ السَّاكِنَيْنِ، وَكُسِرَتِ الْكَافُ لِتَدُلَّ عَلَى الْيَاءِ الْمَحْذُوفَةِ، فَلَمَّا انْكَسَرَتِ الْكَافُ صَارَتْ وَاوُ الْمَفْعُولِ يَاءً.
text.en: You say in the passive participle of the hollow maqūlun “said”; its origin is maqwūlun, and it was treated as we have said. You say in the verbs with yāʾ makīlun “measured”; the origin is makyūlun: the vowel of the yāʾ was moved to the kāf, then the yāʾ was dropped because two unvowelled letters met, and the kāf was given a kasra to point to the dropped yāʾ; and when the kāf had a kasra, the wāw of the passive participle became yāʾ.

text.original: وَإِذَا اجْتَمَعَتِ الْوَاوَانِ، الْأُولَى سَاكِنَةٌ وَالثَّانِيَةُ مُتَحَرِّكَةٌ، فَأُدْغِمَتِ الْأُولَى فِي الثَّانِيَةِ، نَحْوُ: مَغْزُوٌّ، وَالْأَصْلُ مَغْزُووٌ. وَإِذَا اجْتَمَعَ الْوَاوُ وَالْيَاءُ، وَالْأُولَى سَاكِنَةٌ وَالثَّانِيَةُ مُتَحَرِّكَةٌ، قُلِبَتِ الْوَاوُ يَاءً، وَكُسِرَ مَا قَبْلَ الْأُولَى لِيَصِحَّ الْيَاءُ، وَأُدْغِمَتِ الْيَاءُ فِي الْيَاءِ، نَحْوُ: مَرْمِيٌّ وَمَخْشِيٌّ، وَالْأَصْلُ مَرْمُويٌ وَمَخْشُويٌ.
text.en: When two wāws meet, the first unvowelled and the second vowelled, the first is assimilated into the second, as maghzuwwun “raided”; the origin is maghzūwun. When wāw and yāʾ meet, the first unvowelled and the second vowelled, the wāw is turned into yāʾ, the letter before the first is given a kasra so that the yāʾ should be sound, and the yāʾ is assimilated into the yāʾ, as marmiyyun “thrown” and makhshiyyun “feared”; the origin is marmūyun and makhshūyun.

lessons.title: Command and prohibition of the weak verbs
body: The command to the absent of the hollow verb: li-yaqul, from li-yaqūl. In jazm the lām is quiescent; the long ū meets it; two quiescent letters cannot meet, so the long vowel is shortened. The command to the one present: qul, from uqwul. “The vowel of the wāw moved to the qāf; the wāw dropped because it met the quiescent lām; and the hamza dropped because the qāf now had a vowel.”

“And in the dual you say qūlā, because the wāw is restored by the vowel of the lām.” Once the lām has a vowel (the alif of the dual needs it), there are no longer two quiescent letters, and the long ū comes back. So qul for one man and qūlā for two: the weak letter drops when the lām is quiescent and returns when it takes a vowel.

The defective verb: li-yaghzu and li-yarmi, and to the one present ughzu and irmi, “by dropping the wāw and the yāʾ, because the jazm of the defective verb, and its pause, is the dropping of the last letter of the verb”. This is the sign of jazm by dropping that the Ājurrūmiyya named; here are its forms.

One more rule for the defective verb with wāw: in the passive present, command and prohibition, the wāw becomes a yāʾ, “because they are branches of the past”, and in the passive past the wāw becomes a yāʾ for being at the end after a kasra: ghuziya, from ghuziwa. The passive takes its yāʾ from the past and keeps it in its other forms.

terms.en: the pause; the imperative is built on it
dropping the last root letter: the jazm of the defective
the return of the dropped letter: qūlā

examples.en: li-yaqul, from li-yaqūl; qul, from uqwul
qūlā, “say! (to two)”: the wāw returns when the lām takes a vowel
the defective in jazm: its last letter dropped
ghuziya, “he was raided”, from ghuziwa

tasks.prompt: Explain step by step how uqwul becomes qul.
tasks.answer: The ḍamma of the wāw moves to the qāf; the wāw, now quiescent, drops because it meets the quiescent lām; the qāf now has a vowel, so the hamza of joining is no longer needed and drops: qul.

tasks.prompt: Why is it qul for one man but qūlā for two?
tasks.answer: In qul the lām is quiescent, so the long ū had to drop before it. In qūlā the lām has a vowel for the alif of the dual; there are no longer two quiescent letters, and the wāw returns.

tasks.prompt: What is the sign of jazm in li-yarmi and irmi?
tasks.answer: The dropping of the last root letter (the yāʾ of yarmī): the jazm and the pause of the defective verb are the dropping of its lām.

quiz.prompt: What is the base of qul?
quiz.explanation: The imperative pattern ufʿul on q-w-l.

quiz.prompt: Why does the hamza drop in qul?
options: It is a hamza of the root
The qāf now has a vowel
quiz.explanation: A hamza of joining is needed only before a quiescent letter.

quiz.prompt: Qūlā has a long ū because…
options: the lām has a vowel, so the wāw returns
quiz.explanation: The wāw is restored by the vowel of the lām.

quiz.prompt: The command to one man of ghazā is…
quiz.explanation: The wāw dropped in the pause.

quiz.prompt: Li-yarmi shows jazm by…
quiz.explanation: The jazm of the defective verb.

quiz.prompt: Ghuziya comes from…
quiz.explanation: A final wāw after kasra becomes yāʾ.

quiz.prompt: Why do the passive forms of a defective verb with wāw have a yāʾ?
options: They follow the passive past, their source
quiz.explanation: “Because they are branches of the past.”

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي أَمْرِ الْغَائِبِ مِنَ الْأَجْوَفِ: لِيَقُلْ، وَالْأَصْلُ لِيَقُولْ، وَفِي الْمُخَاطَبِ: قُلْ، وَالْأَصْلُ اُقْوُلْ، فَنُقِلَتْ حَرَكَةُ الْوَاوِ إِلَى الْقَافِ، وَحُذِفَتِ الْوَاوُ لِسُكُونِهَا وَسُكُونِ اللَّامِ، وَحُذِفَتِ الْهَمْزَةُ لِحَرَكَةِ الْقَافِ. وَتَقُولُ فِي التَّثْنِيَةِ: قُولَا، لِانْعِقَادِ الْوَاوِ بِحَرَكَةِ اللَّامِ.
text.en: You say in the command to the absent from the hollow li-yaqul “let him say”; the origin is li-yaqūl; and to the one addressed qul “say!”; the origin is uqwul: the vowel of the wāw was moved to the qāf, the wāw was dropped because it and the lām were unvowelled, and the hamza was dropped because the qāf was vowelled. You say in the dual qūlā, because the wāw is restored by the vowel of the lām.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي أَمْرِ النَّاقِصِ: لِيَغْزُ وَلِيَرْمِ، وَفِي أَمْرِ الْمُخَاطَبِ: اُغْزُ وَارْمِ، بِحَذْفِ الْوَاوِ وَالْيَاءِ؛ لِأَنَّ جَزْمَ النَّاقِصِ وَوَقْفَهُ سُقُوطُ لَامِ فِعْلِهِ. وَفِي النَّاقِصِ الْوَاوِيِّ تُقْلَبُ الْوَاوُ يَاءً فِي الْمُسْتَقْبَلِ وَالْأَمْرِ وَالنَّهْيِ الْمَجْهُولَاتِ؛ لِأَنَّهُنَّ فُرُوعُ الْمَاضِي، وَفِي الْمَاضِي الْمَجْهُولِ يَصِيرُ الْوَاوُ يَاءً لِتَطَرُّفِهَا وَانْكِسَارِ مَا قَبْلَهَا، نَحْوُ: غُزِيَ، وَالْأَصْلُ غُزِوَ.
text.en: You say in the imperative of the defective li-yaghzu and wa-li-yarmi, and in the imperative to the one addressed ughzu and wa-irmi, by dropping the wāw and the yāʾ; for the jazm and the pause of the defective is the falling away of the lām of its verb. In the defective with wāw, the wāw is turned into yāʾ in the passive future, imperative and prohibition, because they are branches of the past; and in the passive past the wāw becomes yāʾ because it is at the end and the letter before it has a kasra, as ghuziya “it was raided”; the origin is ghuziwa.

lessons.title: The mithāl: the wāw that drops
body: The verb weak in its fāʾ: “its fāʾ drops in the active present, command and prohibition if its fāʾ is a wāw, from three bābs”. Faʿala yafʿilu: waʿada yaʿidu, “to promise”. Faʿala yafʿalu: wahaba yahabu, “to give”. Faʿila yafʿilu: waritha yarithu, “to inherit”. In each the wāw of the root is gone from the present.

The command and the prohibition follow the present: ʿid, lā taʿid; hab, lā tahab; rith, lā tarith. These are among the shortest words of Arabic: a whole root reduced to two letters, the wāw dropped at the start and the last letter quiescent. ʿId, “promise!”, is yaʿidu without its prefix.
“And the wāw may drop from the bāb of faʿila yafʿalu in two words”: waṭiʾa yaṭaʾu, “to tread”, and wasiʿa yasaʿu, “to be wide, to contain”. Outside these three bābs and two words the wāw stays.

Why does the wāw drop? The commentaries explain that a wāw between the yāʾ of the prefix and a kasra is heavy; the Maqṣūd only states where it drops, and its three bābs and two words are what the student must keep. The passive keeps the wāw: the Maqṣūd says “the active” present.

terms.en: the verb weak in its fāʾ
the dropping of the first root letter
the active forms, in which the wāw drops

tasks.prompt: In which three bābs does the wāw of the mithāl drop in the present, and with which examples?
tasks.answer: Faʿala yafʿilu (waʿada yaʿidu), faʿala yafʿalu (wahaba yahabu) and faʿila yafʿilu (waritha yarithu).

tasks.prompt: How many letters does ʿid have, and where are the other root letters?
tasks.answer: Two: ʿayn and dāl. The wāw of the root (w-ʿ-d) dropped in the present yaʿidu, and the prefix is dropped in the imperative.

tasks.prompt: Name the two words of the bāb faʿila yafʿalu in which the wāw drops.
tasks.answer: Waṭiʾa yaṭaʾu, “to tread”, and wasiʿa yasaʿu, “to be wide, contain”.

quiz.prompt: In which forms does the wāw of the mithāl drop?
options: The active present, command and prohibition
quiz.explanation: Yaʿidu, ʿid, lā taʿid.

quiz.prompt: The present of wahaba is…
quiz.explanation: Faʿala yafʿalu, the wāw dropped.

quiz.prompt: The command of waritha is…
quiz.explanation: The present is yarithu, without the wāw; the command drops the prefix: rith.

quiz.prompt: Which is one of the two words of faʿila yafʿalu with the wāw dropped?
quiz.explanation: The book names two words of faʿila yafʿalu that drop the wāw: wasiʿa yasaʿu and waṭiʾa yaṭaʾu.

quiz.prompt: In how many bābs does the wāw drop by rule?
quiz.explanation: Faʿala yafʿilu, faʿala yafʿalu, faʿila yafʿilu.

quiz.prompt: ʿId means…
quiz.explanation: The command of waʿada.

quiz.prompt: Lā tahab means…
quiz.explanation: The prohibition of wahaba.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْمُعْتَلُّ الْمِثَالُ فَتَسْقُطُ فَاءُ فِعْلِهِ فِي الْمُسْتَقْبَلِ وَالْأَمْرِ وَالنَّهْيِ الْمَعْرُوفَاتِ إِذَا كَانَ فَاؤُهُ وَاوًا مِنْ ثَلَاثَةِ أَبْوَابٍ: فَعَلَ يَفْعِلُ بِفَتْحِ الْعَيْنِ فِي الْمَاضِي وَكَسْرِهَا فِي الْغَابِرِ، نَحْوُ: وَعَدَ يَعِدُ، وَفَعَلَ يَفْعَلُ بِفَتْحِ الْعَيْنِ فِي الْمَاضِي وَالْغَابِرِ، نَحْوُ: وَهَبَ يَهَبُ، وَفَعِلَ يَفْعِلُ بِكَسْرِ الْعَيْنِ فِي الْمَاضِي وَالْغَابِرِ، نَحْوُ: وَرِثَ يَرِثُ.
text.en: As for the weak mithāl, the fāʾ of its verb falls away in the active future, imperative and prohibition when its fāʾ is wāw, in three bābs: faʿala yafʿilu, with fatḥa on the ʿayn in the past and kasra in the ghābir, as waʿada yaʿidu “to promise”; faʿala yafʿalu, with fatḥa on the ʿayn in the past and the ghābir, as wahaba yahabu “to give”; and faʿila yafʿilu, with kasra on the ʿayn in the past and the ghābir, as waritha yarithu “to inherit”.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي الْأَمْرِ وَالنَّهْيِ: عِدْ لَا تَعِدْ، وَهَبْ لَا تَهَبْ، رِثْ لَا تَرِثْ. وَقَدْ تَسْقُطُ الْوَاوُ مِنْ بَابِ فَعِلَ يَفْعَلُ بِكَسْرِ الْعَيْنِ فِي الْمَاضِي وَفَتْحِهَا فِي الْغَابِرِ مِنْ لَفْظَيْنِ، نَحْوُ: وَطِئَ يَطَأُ، وَوَسِعَ يَسَعُ.
text.en: You say in the imperative and the prohibition ʿid lā taʿid “promise!, do not promise!”, hab lā tahab “give!, do not give!” and rith lā tarith “inherit!, do not inherit!”. The wāw may also fall away from the bāb of faʿila yafʿalu, with kasra on the ʿayn in the past and fatḥa in the ghābir, in two words: waṭiʾa yaṭaʾu “to tread” and wasiʿa yasaʿu “to have room for”.

lessons.title: The lafīf: rawā and waqā
body: The joined lafīf has its two weak letters side by side, ʿayn and lām. “The rule of its ʿayn is that of the sound verb: it does not change”, as in ṭawā; “and the rule of its lām is that of the lām of the defective verb”: rawā yarwī, “to narrate”, like ramā yarmī; and the command irwi, “by dropping the lām of the verb”, like irmi. Only one of the two weak letters behaves as weak.

The separated lafīf has its weak letters at the start and the end, fāʾ and lām: waqā yaqī, “to protect”. Its fāʾ follows the mithāl, dropping in the present (yaqī, like yaʿidu); its lām follows the defective, dropping in jazm. So the command: qi. “Its fāʾ dropped as in the mithāl, its lām dropped in jazm as in the defective, and the qāf alone was left, with a kasra; and a hāʾ is added in the pause in the masculine singular”: qih.

The other persons of the command: qiyā to two, qū to men, qī to a woman, qīna to women. In qiyā the yāʾ of the root comes back before the alif of the dual; in qū, qī and qīna the ending follows the qāf directly. A word of one letter, qi, is as short as an Arabic verb can be.

The lafīf thus teaches nothing new: it is two rules already learnt, the mithāl's and the defective's, applied together. That is the Maqṣūd's way throughout the chapter: the weak verbs are combinations of a few rules, not a list of exceptions.

terms.en: the joined lafīf: weak ʿayn and lām
the separated lafīf: weak fāʾ and lām
the hāʾ of pause: qih

examples.en: rawā yarwī, “to narrate”; irwi, “narrate!”: the joined lafīf
waqā yaqī, “to protect”; qi, “protect!”: the separated lafīf
qiyā, qū, qī, qīna: the command to two, to men, to a woman, to women

tasks.prompt: Which of the two weak letters of rawā behaves as weak, and how?
tasks.answer: Only the lām: it follows the defective verb (yarwī, irwi). The ʿayn, the wāw, follows the sound verb and does not change.

tasks.prompt: Explain how waqā gives the command qi.
tasks.answer: The fāʾ (wāw) drops in the present, as in the mithāl (yaqī); in the imperative the lām (yāʾ) drops in jazm, as in the defective; only the qāf is left, with its kasra. In the pause a hāʾ is added: qih.

tasks.prompt: Give the command of waqā to two, to men, to a woman and to women.
tasks.answer: Qiyā, qū, qī, qīna.

quiz.prompt: The joined lafīf has weak…
quiz.explanation: In the joined lafīf the weak letters stand side by side, ʿayn and lām: rawā, ṭawā.

quiz.prompt: The ʿayn of the joined lafīf…
options: does not change, like the sound verb
quiz.explanation: Only the lām is treated as weak.

quiz.prompt: The command of rawā is…
quiz.explanation: The lām dropped, as in irmi.

quiz.prompt: The command of waqā to one man is…
quiz.explanation: Fāʾ and lām both dropped.

quiz.prompt: What is added to qi in the pause?
quiz.explanation: Qi is a single letter; in the pause a hāʾ is added to the masculine singular: qih.

quiz.prompt: Qū is the command of waqā to…
quiz.explanation: Qiyā to two, qū to men, qī to a woman.

quiz.prompt: The separated lafīf combines the rules of…
quiz.explanation: Fāʾ as in waʿada, lām as in ramā.

text.original: وَأَمَّا اللَّفِيفُ الْمَقْرُونُ فَحُكْمُ عَيْنِ فِعْلِهِ كَحُكْمِ الصَّحِيحِ لَا تَتَغَيَّرُ، نَحْوُ: طَوَى، وَحُكْمُ لَامِ فِعْلِهِ كَحُكْمِ لَامِ فِعْلِ النَّاقِصِ، مِثْلُ: رَوَى يَرْوِي، وَتَقُولُ فِي الْأَمْرِ مِنْهُ: ارْوِ، بِحَذْفِ لَامِ الْفِعْلِ.
text.en: As for the joined lafīf, the rule of the ʿayn of its verb is like the rule of the sound verb: it does not change, as ṭawā “to fold”; and the rule of the lām of its verb is like the rule of the lām of the defective verb, as rawā yarwī “to relate”; and you say in its imperative irwi “relate!”, by dropping the lām of the verb.

text.original: وَأَمَّا اللَّفِيفُ الْمَفْرُوقُ فَحُكْمُ فَاءِ فِعْلِهِ كَحُكْمِ فَاءِ فِعْلِ الْمُعْتَلِّ، وَحُكْمُ لَامِ فِعْلِهِ كَحُكْمِ لَامِ فِعْلِ النَّاقِصِ، نَحْوُ: وَقَى يَقِي، وَتَقُولُ فِي الْأَمْرِ: قِ، فَحُذِفَتْ فَاءُ فِعْلِهِ كَالْمُعْتَلِّ، وَحُذِفَتْ لَامُ فِعْلِهِ فِي الْجَزْمِ كَالنَّاقِصِ، فَبَقِيَتِ الْقَافُ مَكْسُورَةً، وَزِيدَتِ الْهَاءُ عِنْدَ الْوَقْفِ فِي الْوَاحِدِ الْمُذَكَّرِ.
text.en: As for the separated lafīf, the rule of the fāʾ of its verb is like the rule of the fāʾ of the weak [mithāl] verb, and the rule of the lām of its verb is like the rule of the lām of the defective verb, as waqā yaqī “to guard”; you say in the imperative qi “guard!”: the fāʾ of its verb was dropped as in the weak [mithāl], and the lām of its verb was dropped in jazm as in the defective, so the qāf remained with a kasra; and a hāʾ is added in the pause in the masculine singular.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي التَّثْنِيَةِ: قِيَا، وَفِي الْجَمْعِ: قُوا، وَفِي الْوَاحِدَةِ الْحَاضِرَةِ: قِي، وَفِي جَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ: قِينَ.
text.en: You say in the dual qiyā, in the plural qū, in the singular feminine present qī, and in the feminine plural qīna.

lessons.title: The doubled verb
body: If the ʿayn of the doubled verb is quiescent and its lām vowelled, or both are vowelled, assimilation is required: madda yamuddu, from madada yamdudu; “the vowel of the first dāl moved to the mīm, so the dāl was left quiescent and was assimilated into the second”. If the ʿayn is vowelled and the lām quiescent, assimilation is impossible and both letters show: madadna.

If both are quiescent, as in jazm (lam yamdud, once the vowel of the first dāl has moved to the mīm), “the second is given a vowel and the first is assimilated into it”: lam yamudda. The vowel is a fatḥa, “because the fatḥa is the lightest of the vowels”; it may be a ḍamma, following the ʿayn; or a kasra, “because a quiescent letter, when given a vowel, takes a kasra”. Lam yamudd- has three possible endings.

The command follows. From a verb on yafʿulu: mudda, muddu, muddi, “and the mīm has a ḍamma in all three”, or umdud without assimilation. From yafʿilu: firri and firra, “flee!”, or ifrir. From yafʿalu: ʿaḍḍa and ʿaḍḍi, “bite!”, or iʿḍaḍ. Each bāb allows the vowels that fit it, and every doubled verb allows the unassimilated form as well.

The augmented doubled verb: aḥabba yuḥibbu, “to love”, from aḥbaba yuḥbibu: the vowel of the first bāʾ moved to the ḥāʾ, and the bāʾ was assimilated into the bāʾ. Its command: aḥibba or aḥbib, “with assimilation and without”. “And whenever you assimilate a letter into a letter, you put a shadda in its place.”

terms.en: assimilation required
leaving the two letters apart
the fatḥa is the lightest vowel
the shadda put in place of the assimilated letter

examples.en: madda yamuddu, assimilated; madadna, kept apart
lam yamudda, from lam yamdud: the second dāl given a fatḥa
the command of madda in four ways
aḥabba yuḥibbu, from aḥbaba yuḥbibu; its command assimilated or not

tasks.prompt: Explain how lam yamdud becomes lam yamudda, and give the other vowels allowed on the last dāl with their reasons.
tasks.answer: The vowel of the first dāl moves to the mīm; both dāls are now quiescent; the second is given a vowel and the first is assimilated into it. The vowel is a fatḥa, the lightest; a ḍamma is allowed, following the ʿayn; and a kasra, the vowel a quiescent letter takes when moved.

tasks.prompt: Give the command of madda, farra and ʿaḍḍa in every way the book allows.
tasks.answer: Madda: muddu, mudda, muddi, or umdud. Farra: firri, firra, or ifrir. ʿAḍḍa: ʿaḍḍa, ʿaḍḍi, or iʿḍaḍ.

tasks.prompt: What is the base of yuḥibbu, and what happened?
tasks.answer: Yuḥbibu. The vowel of the first bāʾ moved to the ḥāʾ, and the first bāʾ, now quiescent, was assimilated into the second; a shadda stands in its place: yuḥibbu.

quiz.prompt: When is assimilation impossible in the doubled verb?
options: When the ʿayn is vowelled and the lām quiescent
quiz.explanation: When the lām is quiescent before a vowelled ʿayn, as in madadna, the two letters cannot be assimilated.

quiz.prompt: Why is lam yamudda vowelled with a fatḥa?
options: The fatḥa is the lightest vowel
quiz.explanation: A ḍamma or kasra is allowed too.

quiz.prompt: Which command of madda keeps the dāls apart?
quiz.explanation: Umdud leaves the two dāls apart; mudda, muddu and muddi assimilate them.

quiz.prompt: Which vowels does the book allow in the command of farra?
quiz.explanation: And ifrir without assimilation.

quiz.prompt: What is the base of aḥabba?
quiz.explanation: Aḥabba is afʿala on ḥ-b-b: aḥbaba, with the first bāʾ assimilated into the second.

quiz.prompt: What is put in place of an assimilated letter?
quiz.explanation: “You put a shadda in its place.”

quiz.prompt: The command of ʿaḍḍa without assimilation is…
quiz.explanation: ʿAḍḍa is of the bāb yafʿalu; without assimilation its command is iʿḍaḍ, with the two ḍāds apart.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْمُضَاعَفُ إِذَا كَانَ عَيْنُ فِعْلِهِ سَاكِنَةً وَلَامُهُ مُتَحَرِّكَةً، أَوْ كِلْتَاهُمَا مُتَحَرِّكَتَيْنِ، فَالْإِدْغَامُ فِيهِ لَازِمٌ، نَحْوُ: مَدَّ يَمُدُّ، وَالْأَصْلُ مَدَدَ يَمْدُدُ، فَنُقِلَتْ حَرَكَةُ الدَّالِ الْأُولَى إِلَى الْمِيمِ فَبَقِيَتْ سَاكِنَةً، فَأُدْغِمَتِ الدَّالُ الْأُولَى فِي الثَّانِيَةِ فَصَارَ يَمُدُّ. وَإِذَا كَانَ عَيْنُ فِعْلِهِ مُتَحَرِّكَةً وَلَامُهُ سَاكِنَةً فَالْإِظْهَارُ لَازِمٌ، نَحْوُ: مَدَدْنَ.
text.en: As for the muḍāʿaf, when the ʿayn of its verb is unvowelled and its lām vowelled, or both are vowelled, assimilation in it is necessary, as madda yamuddu “to stretch”; the origin is madada yamdudu: the vowel of the first dāl was moved to the mīm, and it remained unvowelled, so the first dāl was assimilated into the second and it became yamuddu. When the ʿayn of its verb is vowelled and its lām unvowelled, keeping them apart (iẓhār) is necessary, as madadna “they (f.) stretched”.

text.original: وَإِنْ كَانَتَا سَاكِنَتَيْنِ فَحُرِّكَتِ الثَّانِيَةُ وَأُدْغِمَتِ الْأُولَى فِيهَا، نَحْوُ: لَمْ يَمُدَّ، وَالْأَصْلُ لَمْ يَمْدُدْ، فَنُقِلَتْ حَرَكَةُ الدَّالِ الْأُولَى إِلَى الْمِيمِ فَبَقِيَتَا سَاكِنَتَيْنِ، فَحُرِّكَتِ الثَّانِيَةُ وَأُدْغِمَتِ الْأُولَى فِي الثَّانِيَةِ، ثُمَّ فُتِحَتِ الدَّالُ الثَّانِيَةُ لِأَنَّ الْفَتْحَةَ أَخَفُّ الْحَرَكَاتِ، وَيَجُوزُ تَحْرِيكُهَا بِالضَّمِّ تَبَعًا لِلْعَيْنِ، وَبِالْكَسْرِ لِأَنَّ السَّاكِنَ إِذَا حُرِّكَ حُرِّكَ بِالْكَسْرِ، كَمَا ذُكِرَ فِي الْأَمْرِ وَالنَّهْيِ.
text.en: If both are unvowelled, the second is given a vowel and the first is assimilated into it, as lam yamudda; the origin is lam yamdud: the vowel of the first dāl was moved to the mīm, so both remained unvowelled; then the second was given a vowel and the first assimilated into the second; then the second dāl was given a fatḥa, because the fatḥa is the lightest of the vowels; and it may be given a ḍamma, following the ʿayn, or a kasra, because an unvowelled letter, when it is given a vowel, is given a kasra, as was mentioned under the imperative and the prohibition.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي الْأَمْرِ مِنْ يَفْعُلُ بِضَمِّ الْعَيْنِ: مُدُّ بِضَمِّ الدَّالِ، وَمُدَّ بِفَتْحِهَا، وَمُدِّ بِكَسْرِهَا، وَالْمِيمُ مَضْمُومَةٌ فِي الثَّلَاثِ، وَيَجُوزُ امْدُدْ بِالْإِظْهَارِ. وَتَقُولُ مِنْ يَفْعِلُ بِكَسْرِ الْعَيْنِ: فِرِّ بِالْكَسْرِ، وَفِرَّ بِالْفَتْحِ، وَالْفَاءُ مَكْسُورَةٌ فِيهِمَا، وَيَجُوزُ افْرِرْ بِالْإِظْهَارِ.
text.en: You say in the imperative of yafʿulu, with ḍamma on the ʿayn: muddu, with ḍamma on the dāl, mudda, with fatḥa on it, and muddi, with kasra on it, the mīm having a ḍamma in all three; and umdud is allowed, with iẓhār. You say from yafʿilu, with kasra on the ʿayn: firri “flee!”, with kasra, and firra, with fatḥa, the fāʾ having a kasra in both; and ifrir is allowed, with iẓhār.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ مِنْ يَفْعَلُ بِفَتْحِ الْعَيْنِ: عَضَّ بِالْفَتْحِ، وَعَضِّ بِالْكَسْرِ، وَالْعَيْنُ مَفْتُوحَةٌ فِيهِمَا، وَيَجُوزُ اعْضَضْ بِالْإِظْهَارِ. وَتَقُولُ مِنْ أَفْعَلَ: أَحَبَّ يُحِبُّ، وَالْأَصْلُ أَحْبَبَ يُحْبِبُ، فَنُقِلَتْ حَرَكَةُ الْبَاءِ الْأُولَى إِلَى الْحَاءِ، وَأُدْغِمَتِ الْبَاءُ فِي الْبَاءِ. وَتَقُولُ فِي الْأَمْرِ: أَحِبَّ وَأَحْبِبْ بِالْإِدْغَامِ وَالْإِظْهَارِ. وَكُلَّمَا أَدْغَمْتَ حَرْفًا فِي حَرْفٍ أَدْخَلْتَ بَدَلَهُ تَشْدِيدًا.
text.en: You say from yafʿalu, with fatḥa on the ʿayn: ʿaḍḍa “bite!”, with fatḥa, and ʿaḍḍi, with kasra, the ʿayn having a fatḥa in both; and iʿḍaḍ is allowed, with iẓhār. You say from afʿala: aḥabba yuḥibbu “to love”; the origin is aḥbaba yuḥbibu: the vowel of the first bāʾ was moved to the ḥāʾ, and the bāʾ was assimilated into the bāʾ. You say in the imperative aḥibba and aḥbib, with assimilation and with iẓhār. Whenever you assimilate a letter into a letter, you put a shadda in its place.

lessons.title: The hamzated verb
body: A quiescent hamza “may be left as it is, or changed”: after a fatḥa into an alif, after a kasra into a yāʾ, after a ḍamma into a wāw. So yaʾkulu may be said yākulu, yuʾminu yūminu, and iʾdhan, “permit!”, from adhina, īdhan; the print writes them without a hamza on purpose, to show the change.

A vowelled hamza after a vowelled letter does not change: qaraʾa, like a sound verb. After a quiescent letter it may stay, or its vowel may move to the letter before and the hamza drop: “His word, the Most High: wa-sali al-qaryata, whose base is wa-sʾali al-qaryata” (Q 12:82, written وَاسْأَلِ). The vowel of the hamza went to the sīn, and the hamza dropped “because of its sukūn and the sukūn of the lām after it”; “and it has been read both with the hamza and without it”.

Three common verbs make their commands against the rule: khudh, kul and mur, “take!, eat!, command!”, from akhadha, akala and amara, all with hamza as their fāʾ. By the rule, “a quiescent hamza after a ḍamma is made of the kind of the vowel before it”, so the root's hamza would stay as a wāw after the ḍamma of the hamza of joining. “But it is contravened in these examples, for the frequency of their use in the speech of the Arabs.” Short, frequent words wear down.

“The rest of the conjugation of the hamzated verb is by the rule of the sound verb.” The hamza is not a weak letter; it changes only in these cases, and otherwise the hamzated verb is conjugated like naṣara.

tasks.prompt: Explain wa-sali al-qaryata (Q 12:82) from its base.
tasks.answer: The base is wa-sʾali (from saʾala). The hamza has a vowel after a quiescent sīn: its vowel moves to the sīn, and the hamza drops. The verse is read both with the hamza and without it.

tasks.answer: By the rule a quiescent hamza after a ḍamma takes the letter of that vowel, a wāw, and would stay. In these three the Arabs went against the rule and dropped it, with the hamza of joining, because they are used so often.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْمَهْمُوزُ فَإِنْ كَانَتِ الْهَمْزَةُ سَاكِنَةً يَجُوزُ تَرْكُهَا عَلَى حَالِهَا، وَيَجُوزُ قَلْبُهَا: فَإِنْ كَانَ مَا قَبْلَهَا مَفْتُوحًا قُلِبَتْ أَلِفًا، وَإِنْ كَانَ مَكْسُورًا قُلِبَتْ يَاءً، وَإِنْ كَانَ مَضْمُومًا قُلِبَتْ وَاوًا، نَحْوُ: يَاكُلُ وَيُومِنُ وَإِيذَنْ مِنْ أَذِنَ.
text.en: As for the mahmūz, if the hamza is unvowelled, it may be left as it is, and it may be changed: if the letter before it has a fatḥa, it is turned into alif; if a kasra, into yāʾ; if a ḍamma, into wāw, as yākulu “he eats”, yūminu “he believes” and īdhan “permit!”, from adhina.

text.original: وَإِنْ كَانَتِ الْهَمْزَةُ مُتَحَرِّكَةً، فَإِنْ كَانَ مَا قَبْلَهَا حَرْفًا مُتَحَرِّكًا لَا تَتَغَيَّرُ الْهَمْزَةُ كَالصَّحِيحِ، نَحْوُ: قَرَأَ، وَإِنْ كَانَ مَا قَبْلَهَا حَرْفًا سَاكِنًا يَجُوزُ تَرْكُهَا عَلَى حَالِهَا، وَيَجُوزُ نَقْلُ حَرَكَتِهَا إِلَى مَا قَبْلَهَا، مِثَالُهُ قَوْلُهُ تَعَالَى: وَسَلِ الْقَرْيَةَ، وَالْأَصْلُ وَاسْأَلِ الْقَرْيَةَ، فَنُقِلَتْ حَرَكَةُ الْهَمْزَةِ إِلَى السِّينِ، فَحُذِفَتِ الْهَمْزَةُ لِسُكُونِهَا وَسُكُونِ اللَّامِ بَعْدَهَا، وَقَدْ قُرِئَ بِإِثْبَاتِ الْهَمْزَةِ وَتَرْكِهَا.
text.en: If the hamza is vowelled: if the letter before it is vowelled, the hamza does not change, as in the sound verb, as qaraʾa “to read”; if the letter before it is unvowelled, it may be left as it is, and its vowel may be moved to the letter before it. Its example is His word, Most High: wa-sali al-qaryata “and ask the town”; the origin is wa-isʾali al-qaryata: the vowel of the hamza was moved to the sīn, and the hamza was dropped because it and the lām after it were unvowelled. It has been read both with the hamza and without it.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي الْأَمْرِ مِنَ الْأَخْذِ وَالْأَكْلِ وَالْأَمْرِ: خُذْ وَكُلْ وَمُرْ، عَلَى غَيْرِ الْقِيَاسِ؛ لِأَنَّ الْهَمْزَةَ إِذَا كَانَتْ سَاكِنَةً وَمَا قَبْلَهَا مَضْمُومًا يُجْعَلُ مِنْ جِنْسِ حَرَكَةِ مَا قَبْلَهَا، لَكِنْ يُخَالَفُ فِي هَذِهِ الْأَمْثِلَةِ لِكَثْرَةِ الِاسْتِعْمَالِ فِي كَلَامِ الْعَرَبِ. وَبَاقِي تَصْرِيفِ الْمَهْمُوزِ عَلَى قِيَاسِ الصَّحِيحِ.
text.en: You say in the imperative of al-akhdhi “taking”, al-akli “eating” and al-amri “commanding”: khudh “take!”, kul “eat!” and mur “command!”, against the rule; for when the hamza is unvowelled and the letter before it has a ḍamma, it is made of the kind of the vowel before it; but in these examples [the rule] is not followed, because they are so much used in the speech of the Arabs. The rest of the conjugation of the mahmūz follows the rule of the sound verb.

lessons.title: Measure the weak on the sound
body: The book ends with the method that holds it together. “Whenever you find a verb that is not sound, measure it on the sound in all the forms we gave in the chapter of the sound verb. If the rule calls for changing a letter, moving a vowel, or making a letter quiescent, do it; otherwise treat the verb that is not sound like the sound.” Start from the regular pattern; apply the few rules of the weak letters; stop when no rule applies.

This is exactly what the last ten lessons have done. Qāla is faʿala on q-w-l, with one rule; qul is ufʿul with three; ghazaw is faʿalū with two. A student who has the patterns of the Amthila and the Binā and the rules of the Maqṣūd can make the form of any weak verb, and explain it.

But the book is honest about the limits: “in some places the weak letters do not change, though the cause is there”: ʿawira, “to be one-eyed”, iʿtawara, “to take turns”, istawā, “to settle, rise over”. In ʿawira the wāw has a vowel after a fatḥa and yet does not become alif. “Some of them do not change for the soundness of the pattern, and some for another cause.” The book does not say which is which. The usual explanation of ʿawira is its meaning: it stands for iʿwarra, in which the wāw is quiescent and cannot change, so ʿawira keeps it too.

With this the beginner's ṣarf of the Ottoman path is complete: the Amthila's tables on one verb, the Binā's patterns, the Maqṣūd's rules for making and changing forms. Al-ʿIzzī and Marāḥ al-arwāḥ follow at the intermediate stage.

tasks.prompt: State the Maqṣūd's method for any verb that is not sound, in your own words.
tasks.answer: Start from the regular pattern of the sound verb; apply the rules of the weak letters wherever they call for changing a letter, moving a vowel or making a letter quiescent; where no rule applies, leave the verb as the sound pattern gives it.

tasks.prompt: Show the method on qul: from which pattern, and by which rules?
tasks.answer: From the imperative pattern ufʿul on q-w-l: uqwul. The vowel of the wāw moves to the qāf (moving a vowel); the wāw drops before the quiescent lām (two quiescent letters); the hamza drops because the qāf has a vowel.

tasks.prompt: Why does ʿawira keep its wāw, though it has a vowel after a fatḥa?
tasks.answer: The book says only that some such verbs keep their weak letter for the soundness of the pattern and some for another cause. The usual explanation of ʿawira: it stands for iʿwarra, in which the wāw is quiescent and cannot change, so ʿawira keeps it too.

text.original: وَكُلَّمَا وَجَدْتَ فِعْلًا غَيْرَ الصَّحِيحِ فَقِسْهُ عَلَى الصَّحِيحِ فِي جَمِيعِ الْوُجُوهِ الَّتِي ذَكَرْنَاهَا فِي بَابِ الصَّحِيحِ مِنَ التَّصْرِيفِ، فَإِنِ اقْتَضَى الْقِيَاسُ إِلَى إِبْدَالِ حَرْفٍ أَوْ نَقْلٍ أَوْ إِسْكَانٍ فَافْعَلْ، وَإِلَّا فَأَجْرِ الْفِعْلَ الْغَيْرَ الصَّحِيحِ كَالصَّحِيحِ.
text.en: Whenever you find a verb other than sound, measure it against the sound verb in all the forms that we have mentioned in the chapter on the conjugation of the sound verb: if the rule calls for replacing a letter, moving [a vowel] or making [a letter] unvowelled, do so; otherwise treat the verb that is not sound like the sound one.

text.original: وَقَدْ يَكُونُ فِي بَعْضِ الْمَوَاضِعِ لَا تَتَغَيَّرُ الْمُعْتَلَّاتُ فِيهِ مَعَ وُجُودِ الْمُقْتَضِي، نَحْوُ: عَوِرَ، وَاعْتَوَرَ، وَاسْتَوَى، وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ؛ فَبَعْضُهَا لَا يَتَغَيَّرُ لِصِحَّةِ الْبِنَاءِ، وَبَعْضُهَا لِعِلَّةٍ أُخْرَى.
text.en: In some places the weak verbs do not change although the cause is present, as ʿawira “to be one-eyed”, iʿtawara “to take turns” and istawā “to be level”, and others; some of them do not change to keep the form sound, and some for another reason.
